China export controls, a short customer list, and shareholder lawsuits over Design IP add risk. Q3 EDA growth slowed to 8.5%.
None of that has changed my thesis. Management repaid $3.46B of debt in the first half and paid off term loans early. Total liabilities fell 19.6% YoY, and cash rose to $3.61B. Double-digit organic EDA growth is also expected in Q4 and for the full year.
Analysts made 18 upward revisions to fiscal 2027 EPS over the past seven days, with none lower. Royalty-based custom IP, agentic AI workflows, and joint Ansys products sit ahead. Synopsys pays no dividend. The stock has returned 752.46% over ten years. Chips keep getting harder to design, Synopsys sends a bill for every added layer of difficulty, and I expect to own a bigger share of those bills.

Synopsys reportedly eyes Chinese AI labs to speed up chip design
A post on X says the chip-design software maker plans to work with Chinese AI labs, but the company has confirmed no such deals
Synopsys, the electronic design automation company, reportedly plans to collaborate with Chinese AI labs to accelerate chip design.
The claim surfaced in a post on X. Synopsys has made no public announcement of any such partnership, and there are no verified reports linking the company to new deals with Chinese AI labs.
On September 30, 2026, Synopsys and OpenAI announced a multi-year strategic partnership. The goal is a new AI model called GPT-Synopsys.
The model pairs OpenAI’s technology with Synopsys’s electronic design automation tools, known in the industry as EDA.
GPT-Synopsys is designed to let AI agents handle parts of that process on their own. The target tasks include PPA optimization, timing, and verification.
The deal covers joint research and development, licensing, and revenue sharing arrangements, and early engagements for the GPT-Synopsys technology have already started.

The OpenAI tie-up builds on work Synopsys was already doing. The company has been folding AI into its EDA products through two platforms, Autopilot and AgentEngineer.
Synopsys reports more than 50 collaboration projects using those platforms. According to Synopsys, clients have seen up to 50x faster verification closure. The company also reports a 30% enhancement in project productivity.
Synopsys is no stranger to China. In late 2026, the company opened an expanded office and R&D center in Shanghai to better support local partners and customers.
The company’s publicly visible expansion efforts have centered on deepening ties with established semiconductor players, including TSMC, Samsung, Nvidia, and Intel.
A bigger office is not the same as a partnership with Chinese AI labs. The Shanghai investment does not, on its own, confirm the AI lab collaborations described in the X post.
For investors, the confirmed story is the OpenAI partnership, not the China report. GPT-Synopsys gives the company a clear narrative: AI agents that automate parts of chip design, with early engagements already underway under a joint R&D and revenue-sharing structure.
The China claim remains a plan attributed to the company in a social media post, without confirmation from Synopsys itself.

The China claim remains a plan attributed to the company in a social media post, without confirmation from Synopsys itself.

Amazon Web Services is nearing the conclusion of a significant multi-year contract worth over $1 billion with Synopsys. This arrangement includes licensing cutting-edge chip design intellectual property, allowing AWS to amplify its chip development with Synopsys's specialized knowledge. In exchange, Synopsys plans to utilize AWS's robust computing and storage resources for its own processes, aiming for collaborative improvements in advanced AI application design and implementation.
Published On Oct 1, 2026 at 06:00 PM IST
Select ETCIO as Preferred Choice on Google
Synopsys and Amazon Web Services on Wednesday said that Amazon.com's cloud computing unit has entered a multi-year deal worth more than $1 billion to license chip design intellectual property from Synopsys.
Synopsys makes software for designing complex computer chips, helping firms such as Nvidia and Intel decide how to lay out tens of billions of transistors on a few square millimeters of silicon.
But it also increasingly licenses blueprints for parts of a chip, a business that brought in $1.75 billion in revenue in its most recent fiscal year and where it competes against Arm Holdings.
In its early stages, the Synopsys design licensing business focused on common parts of chips where customers found it more cost-effective to license blueprints from Synopsys than to design those parts from scratch. But Synopsys has moved into more complex designs such as computing cores and said the deal on Wednesday will focus on blueprints optimized for specific types of chips.
AWS designs a variety of its own chips, including its Graviton central processors and its Trainium AI chips. The two parties did not specify which AWS chips will use Synopsys blueprints.
As part of the deal, Synopsys will also adopt AWS computing and storage services, as well as Amazon Bedrock to build and deploy AI applications.

Is Synopsys Back from the Dead? EDA Leader Inks Deals With Amazon and OpenAI
Leo Miller - MarketBeat - Sat Oct 10, 7:05AM CDT
Electronic design automation (EDA) company Synopsys (NASDAQ: SNPS) has recently experienced a resurgence in investor sentiment. Through mid-September, Synopsys shares were down more than 20% year-to-date (YTD). Since hitting its September low, the stock has surged more than 30%, putting shares in the green for the year.
Several key developments have aided the stock’s recovery, including an over $1 billion deal with Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) and a development deal with OpenAI. These events signal a potential inflection point in the stock’s trajectory, as Synopsys has so far been a chronic underperformer during the AI investment wave.
Understanding Synopsys’ Underperformance
Synopsys’ poor 2026 performance has been a microcosm of its longer-term underperformance during the AI investment era. From the beginning of 2023 through its September low, Synopsys shares returned just 15%. The stock’s recent surge lifts this figure to approximately 56%, but this is still far from impressive. Over the same period, the S&P 500’s return is approximately 110%, and the S&P 500 tech sector has returned around 225%.
Synopsys’ underperformance has been due to several factors. This includes weakness at Intel’s (NASDAQ: INTC) Foundry business, which has faced delays and has struggled to secure large contracts for its most advanced nodes. This hurts Synopsys’ intellectual property (IP) business because it invested significantly in developing these chips, but it only receives payment once customers commit to Intel’s technology.
There has also been a fear among some investors that AI tools could supplant current EDA tools, hurting demand longer-term. Luckily for Synopsys, the firm’s latest developments push back on these risks.
Synopsys Unlocks New IP Demand With Amazon
Synopsys has signed an over $1 billion deal with Amazon, primarily based around its IP business. The deal includes a $1 billion license fee that allows Amazon to use Synopsys’ IP across multiple generations of its Graviton, Trainium, and Nitro chips. On top of this, Synopsys will receive a customization fee and royalties, which are part of its new application optimized IP (AoIP) business model. Synopsys’ traditional standards-based IP model only includes licensing and nonrecurring engineering fees.
With the AoIP model, Synopsys’ goal is that royalties, where it receives payment for each chip produced, will exceed license fees long-term. This provides much more upside to each AoIP agreement. The Amazon deal also helps mitigate the weakness at Intel’s Foundry because Amazon is already deploying its custom chips at scale, providing more certainty around royalty revenue. However, this applies to future generation chips, meaning royalties will not kick in for over a year from now.
By fiscal year 2030 (FY2030), Synopsys expects to generate $1 billion in AoIP revenue. Importantly, it bases this forecast only on current contracts and commitments, implying room for long-term upside potential. This deal demonstrates the importance of Synopsys’ IP for businesses pursuing long-term custom chip roadmaps. Additionally, the new AoIP model shows the company is exerting pricing power through customization and royalties, a strong positive signal.
OpenAI and Synopsys Partner to Accelerate Chip Development
The company’s deal with OpenAI also has significant implications. Together, the two firms will develop GPT-Synopsys, “a specialized model for chip design that brings together OpenAI's frontier AI with Synopsys' trusted EDA tools and chip design expertise.” Essentially, the companies will train a model that can operate Synopsys’ EDA tools, thereby accelerating the chip development process.
This is important because chip design involves running many experiments and then iterating until engineers find the best design. This creates a bottleneck where humans can only run so many experiments at once. By allowing engineers to autonomously explore a much greater range of designs, OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman argues that companies can shave weeks or months off the design process.
Synopsys argues that this will expand its total addressable market because AI will use more of its EDA tools. This could also accelerate its IP business, as companies can bring newer chips into production faster. The deal also directly pushes back on the idea that AI models will displace EDA tools, as OpenAI itself clearly sees a need to leverage Synopsys’ expertise.
Synopsys Raises Outlook After Finding New Growth Vectors
Amid these developments, Synopsys significantly raised its long-term guidance. Through FY2030, it now expects revenue to increase by a mid-teens compound annual growth rate, up from "double digits" before. The firm also targets an adjusted operating margin of 50% by FY2030, a significant improvement from its prior mid-40% expectation. This implies a large expansion over the coming years, with Synopsys guiding for a 41.5% adjusted operating margin in fiscal year 2026.
Synopsys’ deal with Amazon and its partnership with OpenAI represent two new ways the firm can benefit from AI development. Looking into 2027, it will be important to monitor whether Synopsys sees an uptick in its EDA growth through the OpenAI deal, and if the company can secure more large AoIP customers outside of Amazon. Should the company continue to gain momentum in these areas, it could provide considerable tailwinds for its financials and share price.

Here’s What $10,000 Invested in Synopsys Stock Could Be Worth by 2030
Synopsys builds the software that powers every chip designed for AI, and analysts are practically falling over each other to buy it. But the real question is whether the tailwinds behind this under-the-radar pick can push a modest investment into…
Published October 19, 2026, 9:30am ET · 3 min read
Price Targets desk. Editor: Vandita Jadeja.
The vivid imagery of a circuit board overlaid with an upward-trending graph illustrates the impressive growth and robust performance within the semiconductor industry, as reflected in leading chip funds like SOXQ and SMH. © 24/7 WallSt
Shares of Synopsys (NASDAQ:SNPS | SNPS Price Prediction) recently changed hands at $466.88. So what could a $10,000 investment look like by 2030? Synopsys sells the software that chipmakers use to design their products.
One 24/7 Wall St. podcast host compared it to “the AutoCAD or the CAD of this industry”. As AI chips get more complex, that tools matters more, and that’s the reason to take a longer look at the stock.
What $10,000 Could Grow Into in the Base Case
The figures below use a five-year period ending October 15, 2031. That’s the projected period closest to 2030. The base case puts a $10,000 investment at about $20,481, a total return of 104.81%. That outcome depends on the stock climbing from a projected entry price of $467.11 to a per-share target of $956.68. The annualized return comes to 15.42%.
A quarterly path is also mapped out by the model, and one point on it falls in 2030. The base-case path reaches $899.95 on October 15, 2030, which would make a $10,000 investment worth about $19,266.34. Treat that 2030 figure as illustrative only. It’s a stop on the projected path.
Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios for Your $10,000
The projection’s signal reads buy, at 0.9 confidence, a projected output rather than advice. Over the closer one-year period, its base-case target is $598.21, an upside of 28.07%.
Wall Street analysts are also positive. Their consensus target is $572.17, with 4 strong buy, 19 buy, and 2 hold ratings and no sells.
The more complex a chip, the more design software it takes to build it. In the fiscal third quarter, revenue rose 42.4% from a year earlier to $2.48 billion. Non-GAAP EPS came in at $3.91, beating the $3.67 consensus.
Management then raised its full-year guidance to non-GAAP EPS of $15.04 to $15.10 and said it expects double-digit growth in EDA, its core design-software business. Synopsys has now beaten earnings estimates 4 quarters in a row.
Ansys Adds Simulation, From Single Chips to Full Systems
Ansys adds simulation tools that reach beyond chips into automotive, aerospace, and industrial customers. The company expects Ansys to contribute about $2.98 billion of fiscal 2026 revenue. Chief executive Sassine Ghazi put it this way: “One year after the transformational acquisition of Ansys, we are executing with focus, extending our leadership and gaining momentum.”
Management has also pointed to a $400 million revenue-synergy opportunity in semiconductor multi-physics, with monetization expected to start in fiscal 2027.
At last count, 20 customers were evaluating Synopsys’ agentic AI design tools. Ghazi described a pricing model that would move from “subscription license that our customer has for the human engineers” to “subscription plus consumption for the agents.”
If customers adopt it widely, that model could lift earnings per customer. Margins are already strong: the non-GAAP operating margin reached 41.6% last quarter.
The bear case still assumes gains, but nothing ensures them. Synopsys’ guidance assumes no further changes to U.S. export controls or Entity List restrictions, and new limits on China could reduce sales.
The company also carries about $10 billion of long-term debt from the Ansys deal, and it has planned restructuring charges for the fiscal fourth quarter. Additional risks come from a few large customers that account for a big share of sales, tough competition in EDA, and the chance that Ansys synergies fall short.
Expect a rough ride, too. The stock has a beta of 1.208, meaning it tends to swing more than the market overall. Shares fell 7.12% over the past week after climbing 22.4% over the past month, and they’re down 0.6% so far this year.
Valuation is another factor: the stock trades at about 87x trailing earnings and 23x forward earnings. If AI-related demand cools off, the share price could drop quickly.
Your $10,000 by 2030: A Range of Outcomes
Over the five-year projected period, a $10,000 stake in Synopsys ranges from about $13,766 in the bear case to $24,581 in the bull case, with the base case landing at $20,481.
To track the thesis, watch Ansys synergy progress, adoption of the AI agent tools, and any changes to export rules. The projection is not investment advice, and actual returns could be higher or lower than any scenario shown here.

Synopsys Details Growth Strategy and Long-term Financial Model at 2026 Investor Day
Leading portfolio of engineering solutions positions Synopsys to capitalize on the continued expansion of digital and physical AI and the AI-driven transformation of engineering.
Updates long-term growth targets to reflect accelerating revenue and expanding non-GAAP operating margins. Company expects fiscal year 2027 revenue growth of approximately 15% year over year to $11.15 billion at the midpoint of guidance range.
After investing in the business, Synopsys expects to return up to 50% of free cash flow to shareholders via share repurchases; with intent to repurchase approximately $1 billion in shares over the coming months, subject to market conditions.
SUNNYVALE, Calif.
, Sept. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Synopsys, Inc. (NASDAQ: SNPS) today detailed its long-term growth strategy and sustainable long-term financial model at its 2026 Investor Day in New York. Management outlined how AI is driving demand, transforming engineering, unlocking new business models and accelerating growth across the portfolio. A replay of the presentation will be available on Synopsys'investor relations website.
Synopsys President and CEO, Sassine Ghazi, said: "AI is creating multiple, reinforcing growth engines for Synopsys. The acceleration of frontier intelligence is fueling an unprecedented demand for compute power while increasing system complexity. Simultaneously, purpose-built silicon is reshaping the IP market, while Physical AI and agentic workflows are driving deeper integration of our trusted tools. Together, these forces are expanding our addressable market, increasing consumption of our technology, and creating new, recurring revenue streams."
Highlights from executive presentations include:
Silicon IP Business Expands to Serve Growing Demand for Special-purpose Silicon
Synopsys is expanding beyond traditional standards-based IP into application-optimized IP (AOIP), helping customers develop differentiated silicon tailored to specific workloads and system architectures. As AI drives demand for custom silicon across hyperscalers and system companies, Synopsys is leveraging its interface IP leadership, system expertise, and engineering scale to deliver optimized IP subsystems and platforms that accelerate time-to-market while improving performance and efficiency.
This 'Factory 2' IP model expands Synopsys' value capture per design win and increases its participation in the long-term growth of custom silicon and AI infrastructure. Demonstrating early momentum for the new IP business model, the company has secured multiple AOIP customers spanning compute, ASIC, and AI connectivity architectures. This includes an IP agreement with Amazon, which was announced today.
Powering the Next Frontier of AI-Driven Design
Ghazi today also explained the company's strategy to create and capture value in the delivery of AI-powered engineering solutions and announced a groundbreaking partnership with OpenAI to collaborate as preferred partners to develop and deliver GPT-Synopsys, a specialized model for chip design that brings together OpenAI's frontier AI with Synopsys' trusted EDA tools and chip design expertise.
Synopsys is advancing the next frontier of AI-driven design and simulation with a strategy that enables customers to adopt its agentic AI portfolio in the way that best fits their engineering environment. Customers can deploy the full Synopsys Autopilot platform, integrate Synopsys agents into their own AI platforms, or leverage frontier AI models optimized for specialized engineering workflows. Across all approaches, Synopsys provides the trusted engineering context, domain-specific agents, and ground-truth execution engines that power the development of the world's most advanced products. This flexible model expands Synopsys' opportunity to participate across the emerging AI engineering ecosystem while creating multiple avenues to monetize AI-driven engineering through a combination of subscription and consumption-based models across tools, agents and platform.
Synopsys Fiscal 2027 and Long-term Financial Outlook
Synopsys provided financial guidance for fiscal year 2027 and a comprehensive multi-year financial framework through fiscal year 2030. The company also announced its intent to repurchase approximately $1 billion of Synopsys shares over the coming months, subject to market conditions, underscoring confidence in its long-term cash generation.
Shelagh Glaser, Synopsys CFO, said, "Our updated financial framework reflects confidence in both our growth trajectory and our ability to scale efficiently while helping customers re-engineer their engineering to accelerate AI-powered products. We remain focused on disciplined execution, converting growth into expanding margins and strong free cash flow, while continuing to invest in innovation and deliver sustainable long-term value for our shareholders."

Non-GAAP operating margin is non-GAAP operating income for a period divided by revenue for the same period

Can Synopsys' AI-Focused Design IP Strategy Drive Growth?
Thu, October 15, 2026 at 8:49 AM CDT 3 min read
Synopsys' SNPS Design IP includes logic libraries, embedded memories, wired interface IP, memory interface IP and security IP. In the third quarter of fiscal 2026, Design IP accounted for 19.1% of total revenues and increased 11% year over year, while the adjusted operating margin improved to 26.5%.
Synopsys holds a leading position in interface and foundation IP. The business is increasingly focused on areas benefiting from AI-driven semiconductor complexity. Synopsys said demand for high-speed interconnect IP is accelerating because of AI's massive data requirements.
Synospys' standards-based IP that can be developed once and licensed repeatedly across customers and applications is gaining traction. Its portfolio includes high-speed interface, memory and die-to-die connectivity IP, which are increasingly important as AI systems require higher bandwidth, faster data transfer and more complex chip architectures.
IP business is on track to double year over year, with cumulative design wins exceeding 100. In automotive, the company maintained a design-win rate above 90% for three consecutive quarters as advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) transitioned to 5-nanometer and 3-nanometer technologies. Its USB IP portfolio has also surpassed $2 billion in lifetime bookings.
SNPS' also focuses on developing differentiated IP subsystems and enabling custom silicon solutions tailored to customers' workloads and architectures. Hyperscalers, ASIC vendors, foundries and semiconductor companies are seeking deeper engineering collaboration to accelerate chip development through this model.
Synopsys operates in a highly competitive market, with major rivals, including Cadence Design Systems Inc. CDNS and Keysight Technologies KEYS. These companies serve different stages of the electronic and IC design lifecycle, offering specialized tools and solutions that help customers improve product development, design efficiency and testing.
Keysight Technologies competes primarily across electronic design, measurement and testing, with software and solutions covering areas such as electromagnetic analysis, circuit simulation and hardware verification. Meanwhile, Cadence Design Systems is benefiting from increasing design complexity and growing customer investments in AI-powered automation.
Cadence is also strengthening its position through its expanding Cadence.ai portfolio. New offerings, including AgentStack, ChipStack, ViraStack and InnoStack AI Super Agents, are broadening the company's AI capabilities across the design workflow and could help Cadence maintain its momentum as AI adoption accelerates.
Synopsys' shares have appreciated 19.3% in the past month, outperforming the Zacks Computer and Technology sector's return of 2.2%.
The outperformance in the stock price led to a premium valuation, with SNPS stock trading at a P/S multiple of 8.44X, much above the industry P/E multiple of 6.37X. The premium valuation is further established by a Zacks Value Score of F.

Synopsys is Hot Again But a Pattern Has Emerged
Synopsys has beaten earnings estimates three times this year, yet shareholders have walked away from each report with less than they started. A chart pattern that keeps repeating raises a pointed question about whether strong fundamentals can ever outrun the…
Published October 6, 2026, 8:45am ET · 3 min read
© krystiannawrocki / E+ via Getty Images
Synopsys (NASDAQ:SNPS | SNPS Price Prediction) trades at $488.47. The chip-design software leader is rallying again, and its 2026 chart has already shown three distinct peaks. Each of those peaks faded.
Synopsys leads electronic design automation (EDA), the software chipmakers use to design and verify semiconductors. It also licenses silicon IP. The roughly $35B Ansys acquisition turned it into a silicon-to-systems engineering provider. Shares rose 16.97% in a week, and Barron’s named it the top stock in the Nasdaq 100 during one recent session.
Three Beat-and-Raise Quarters Power the AI Design Story
Fiscal Q3 revenue reached $2.48B, up 42.4% YoY. Non-GAAP EPS came in at $3.91 against a $3.67 consensus. Management raised full-year guidance for the second straight quarter, to non-GAAP EPS of $15.04 to $15.10. Design IP returned to growth, rising about 11% to $474 million. EDA growth is expected to speed up to double digits.
New products give the story more room to run. Multiphysics Fusion, the first joint Synopsys-Ansys product, delivered up to 10x faster design closure for early customers and should start adding to EDA growth in 2027. Synopsys is also pursuing license-plus-royalty deals with AI customers (the broader AI expansion extends well past the chipmakers themselves, something we covered across power, cooling, and infrastructure suppliers in a free report here). At a forward P/E of 23, investors are paying that multiple for ~$2.6B in guided free cash flow.
Every Earnings Beat This Year Ended in a Selloff
On average, the stock fell 2.35% the day after an earnings beat. Thirty days after the Q1, Q2, and Q3 reports, shares were down 10.06%, 7.19%, and 10.71%. Strong results have repeatedly failed to hold the stock up.
Debt still remains near $10 billion. Amortization of Ansys intangible assets drags GAAP EPS guidance down to $3.84 to $4.08, which leaves a trailing P/E of 86. Backlog slipped slightly from the prior quarter, and Morgan Stanley (NYSE:MS) issued an earlier downgrade that warned of slowing growth. Export-control risk also remains unmeasured.
Strong Execution Meets a Stock That Keeps Round-Tripping
Margins of 41.6%, early debt paydown, and Ansys synergies running ahead of schedule all point to further upside. Repeated post-earnings drops and a still-heavy balance sheet support the bear case. Several key growth drivers, including royalties and joint products, are still in early adoption.
Wall Street Sees 16.6% Upside, but Shares Trail the Market
The consensus target of $569.78 implies 16.6% upside from current levels across 25 analysts. Price targets are one input and come with no guarantee.
The stock gained 24.03% over the past month, compared with 0.61% for the S&P 500. Year to date, Synopsys is up just 3.99%, while the index has risen 13.63%. Its 52-week range runs from $362.55 to $539.48.
Fiscal Q4 Will Show Whether the Pattern Breaks
Synopsys trades at $488.47 heading into its next report.
The fiscal Q4 report is the next real test. Guidance calls for revenue of $2.53B to $2.58B and non-GAAP EPS of $4.10 to $4.16. A beat that holds for a full month, followed by a move above $539.48, would signal a break from the pattern.
Downside risks would build if Design IP stalls, EDA growth misses double digits, or export rules tighten. Each quarter, watch IP momentum, debt reduction, and signed royalty contracts.
The rally could continue. A fourth peak would carry its own risk, since the stock has fallen after each earnings report this year. Synopsys has earned attention, and the next test is whether it can hold a rally.

OpenAI and Synopsys Announce GPT-Synopsys: Frontier Intelligence to Revolutionize Chip Design
Companies form strategic partnership to dramatically advance and accelerate semiconductor innovation
News Highlights:
Companies sign multi-year agreement to collaborate as preferred partners to develop and deliver GPT-Synopsys, a specialized model for chip design that brings together OpenAI's frontier AI with Synopsys' trusted EDA tools and chip design expertise
OpenAI to license Synopsys' trusted electronic design automation (EDA) tools for development of the specialized model
Synopsys & OpenAI to closely collaborate on R&D and joint go-to-market initiatives with a shared revenue framework
SAN FRANCISCO and SUNNYVALE, Calif., Sept. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Synopsys (Nasdaq: SNPS) and OpenAI today announced a strategic partnership that brings together OpenAI's advanced AI capabilities with Synopsys' industry-leading EDA tools and agentic AI capabilities to revolutionize the design of semiconductors. The companies signed an expansive, multi-year agreement to jointly develop GPT-Synopsys, a specialized model, optimized to use Synopsys EDA tools to perform semiconductor design workflows. The agreement includes a revenue sharing arrangement and go-to-market collaboration to jointly make GPT-Synopsys available to customers worldwide.
Today, agentic AI technologies connect general-purpose models to EDA tools to run chip-design workflows. The next leap, with this partnership, is to make frontier models experts in using EDA tools: learning to run the tools as expert engineers, interpreting their outputs, and iteratively optimizing designs using the tools. This integration will make the model a native expert user and enable engineers to explore more design alternatives and optimize power, performance and area (PPA) to rapidly deliver more sophisticated designs.
"The future of semiconductor engineering requires dramatic acceleration of the chip design process without compromising PPA or first-time-right silicon. This agreement will expand access to Synopsys' advanced design capabilities and the underlying, ground-truth engineering tools required to bring increasingly complex chips to market," said Sassine Ghazi, president and CEO of Synopsys. "Together with OpenAI, we're bringing frontier intelligence to chip design to help more companies develop and accelerate advanced silicon, while maintaining the rigor and trust required for manufacturing success."
"We're using our most advanced technology to improve the systems that power AI," said Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI. "With Synopsys, we're bringing that work to chip design, helping engineers explore more designs and get to a working chip faster. By helping them build better chips, we can build better AI and bring it to more people."
GPT-Synopsys to Revolutionize AI-native Chip Design
GPT-Synopsys brings together OpenAI frontier models with Synopsys' EDA technology and domain expertise, enabling the specialized model to reason about chip design and verification, and to directly operate Synopsys' tools. Engineers will delegate design objectives—from PPA optimization to timing and verification closure—with agents running tools, interpreting results, implementing changes, and iterating toward verified outcomes for engineer review. GPT-Synopsys will run on OpenAI-hosted infrastructure, will be designed to interoperate with customer agent harness systems, and will be deeply integrated with Synopsys.ai and the Synopsys Autopilot, agentic AI platform. Early technology engagements are underway with leading semiconductor customers.
The joint service offering will provide the bundled compute, model, and licenses, while ensuring customer-specific design data is protected. GPT-Synopsys will feature enterprise-grade security, governance, and access controls. Customer data is not used to train the model, is encrypted at rest and in transit, and can be managed through configurable retention, audit and permission controls.
Synopsys, Inc. (Nasdaq: SNPS) is the leader in engineering solutions from silicon to systems, enabling customers to rapidly innovate AI-powered products. We deliver industry-leading silicon design, IP, simulation and analysis solutions, and design services. We partner closely with customers across a broad range of industries to maximize their R&D capability and productivity, powering innovation today that ignites the ingenuity of tomorrow. Learn more at www.synopsys.com.

Synopsys, Inc. (SNPS) is Attracting Investor Attention: Here is What You Should Know
Thu, October 15, 2026 at 7:00 AM CDT 5 min read
Synopsys (SNPS) is one of the stocks most watched by Zacks.com visitors lately. So, it might be a good idea to review some of the factors that might affect the near-term performance of the stock.
Shares of this maker of software used to test and develop chips have returned +26.8% over the past month versus the Zacks S&P 500 composite's +2.1% change. The Zacks Computer - Software industry, to which Synopsys belongs, has gained 3.9% over this period. Now the key question is: Where could the stock be headed in the near term?
Although media reports or rumors about a significant change in a company's business prospects usually cause its stock to trend and lead to an immediate price change, there are always certain fundamental factors that ultimately drive the buy-and-hold decision.
Rather than focusing on anything else, we at Zacks prioritize evaluating the change in a company's earnings projection. This is because we believe the fair value for its stock is determined by the present value of its future stream of earnings.
We essentially look at how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to reflect the impact of the latest business trends. And if earnings estimates go up for a company, the fair value for its stock goes up. A higher fair value than the current market price drives investors' interest in buying the stock, leading to its price moving higher. This is why empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.
For the current quarter, Synopsys is expected to post earnings of $4.10 per share, indicating a change of +41.4% from the year-ago quarter. The Zacks Consensus Estimate has changed -0.5% over the last 30 days.
For the current fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $15.13 points to a change of +17.2% from the prior year. Over the last 30 days, this estimate has changed -0.2%.
For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $18.26 indicates a change of +20.7% from what Synopsys is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has changed +4.8%.
Having a strong externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, offers a more conclusive picture of a stock's price direction in the near term, since it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. Due to the size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, Synopsys is rated Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy).
The chart below shows the evolution of the company's forward 12-month consensus EPS estimate:
12-month consensus EPS estimate for SNPS
Even though a company's earnings growth is arguably the best indicator of its financial health, nothing much happens if it cannot raise its revenues. It's almost impossible for a company to grow its earnings without growing its revenue for long periods. Therefore, knowing a company's potential revenue growth is crucial.
In the case of Synopsys, the consensus sales estimate of $2.56 billion for the current quarter points to a year-over-year change of +13.5%. The $9.72 billion and $11.14 billion estimates for the current and next fiscal years indicate changes of +37.8% and +14.6%, respectively.

HSBC Upgrades Synopsys to Buy, Sees 28% Earnings Growth Through 2028
HSBC just flipped its rating on Synopsys with a price target that towers above Wall Street consensus, and the reasoning behind it reframes the chip design giant as something the market may not have priced in yet.
Published September 25, 2026, 10:15am ET · 3 min read
Price Targets desk. Editor: Vandita Jadeja.
Financial data and an upward arrow are overlaid on a computer processor socket, illustrating the complex interplay between technology and market trends impacting investments in companies like Broadcom. © Shutterstock
HSBC analyst Frank Lee upgraded Synopsys (NASDAQ:SNPS | SNPS Price Prediction) to buy from hold and raised his price target to $700 from $490. Lee argues that a change in the chip design software leader’s business model could lift annual earnings growth from 7% to 28% through 2028.
Synopsys stock rose 4.38% in premarket trading to $443.50. The analyst upgrade presents Synopsys as an AI growth story, and near-term volatility remains a real risk.
HSBC’s Royalty Thesis Could Reset Synopsys’ Growth Curve
In a research note, Lee said the new business model will turn Synopsys from a “slow-growth software play to a high-growth AI beneficiary,” with the faster earnings growth “creating significant re-rating potential.” He sees the design intellectual property royalty model as the main driver of that earnings growth.
Management has described the same shift. On the third-quarter call, the chief executive said Synopsys is in advanced talks to move from a traditional IP license to “a license plus a royalty” with customers that include hyperscalers and ASIC vendors. He added, “We are in active discussions with multiple Factory 2 customers.”
Design IP revenue reached $474 million, up about 11% year-over-year. The die-to-die business is “on pace to double year over year,” and Synopsys won more than 95% of PCIe 7 opportunities.
Company Snapshot: Synopsys One Year After Ansys
Synopsys is a leading provider of electronic design automation (EDA) software and semiconductor IP. It expanded into wider engineering software when its $35B Ansys acquisition closed in fiscal Q3 2025.
Fiscal Q3 2026 revenue rose 42.4% YoY to $2.48B. Non-GAAP EPS came in at $3.91, beating the $3.67 consensus, and the non-GAAP operating margin was 41.6%. Management raised its full-year guidance to revenue of $9.69B to $9.74B and non-GAAP EPS of $15.04 to $15.10. Backlog stood at $10.9 billion.
Why Wall Street Is Rethinking Synopsys Right Now
Shares have gained 16.35% over the past week but remain down 5.58% year to date. The stock trades at about 23x forward earnings, compared with a trailing P/E near 72.
Analysts’ estimates are moving higher. The consensus fiscal 2027 EPS estimate rose to $17.5259 from $17.2343 90 days ago.
Over the past 30 days, there were 17 up updates and just 1 down updates. HSBC’s $700 target is well above the consensus target of $545.55. Synopsys also announced an agentic AI partnership with TSMC (NYSE:TSM) this week.
Synopsys offers retirement-focused investors exposure to AI chip design complexity through recurring software and IP revenue. The stock pays no dividend, so any return depends on earnings growth.
The risks are real:
Export controls and Entity List restrictions
Key signals to watch include signed Factory 2 royalty deals and the updates to the long-term IP growth outlook that management has promised for Investor Day.
The royalty shift is really an AI infrastructure story, since Synopsys gets paid every time a hyperscaler or ASIC vendor produces new silicon (we featured seven companies riding the same expansion, outside the chipmakers themselves, in a free report here: 7 Stocks Powering the AI Boom (That Aren’t Chipmakers)).

Synopsys (SNPS) Adopts AI Chipmaking Libraries For Semiconductor Workflows
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 1:15 PM CDT 3 min read
Synopsys (NasdaqGS:SNPS) is adopting NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries and the cuPotential library for AI-driven semiconductor manufacturing workflows.
The collaboration focuses on using NVIDIA's AI platform to help automate and optimize chip design and fabrication processes.
Synopsys is adding NVIDIA to a growing list of AI partners, alongside recent agreements involving OpenAI and Amazon.
Synopsys' move to CUDA-X and cuPotential fits into a broader AI-defined fab trend that deeper research helps explain. We have also flagged 2 warning signs for Synopsys.
This push into NVIDIA-powered AI workflows is not unique to Synopsys, and other chip and tooling vendors are exposed to the same theme 92 AI infrastructure stocks.
NasdaqGS:SNPS Earnings & Revenue Growth as at Oct 2026
Synopsys builds design IP and software that underpin how chips are conceived and verified. Closer integration with NVIDIA's AI stack plugs its tools directly into the workflows of semiconductor and electronics customers that rely heavily on accelerated computing.
2 things going right for Synopsys that this headline doesn't cover.
How NVIDIA CUDA-X feeds Synopsys' AI-first Narrative
The Synopsys Narrative hinges on AI-driven design tools, high-value IP and Ansys-powered simulation becoming an integrated engineering platform, and this NVIDIA move ties directly into that AI and simulation story.
"Analysts expect Synopsys to continue building on AI driven EDA, IP and Ansys powered simulation demand as customers pursue more complex, multi die architectures and agentic AI based design flows..."
See how the full story points towards a $570 fair value for Synopsys.
Adopting NVIDIA CUDA-X and cuPotential directly supports the catalyst that Synopsys can turn AI-assisted and agentic design into a full workflow, not just a feature. By wiring its tools into NVIDIA's acceleration stack, the business pushes its EDA and Ansys simulation closer to where AI-heavy chip projects actually run, alongside peers such as Cadence and Siemens.
This update also puts pressure on a softer part of the thesis: the slower IP segment and the integration risk around Ansys. Tighter alignment with NVIDIA makes execution stakes higher, because missed Ansys cost synergies or weaker IP traction would matter more if rivals match similar GPU-accelerated flows and erode any AI-defined fab advantage.
To make sense of this kind of AI tooling news for Synopsys, you need a clear view of where management is trying to steer the business, which is exactly what a Narrative lays out.
The missing question on Synopsys: where do the long range forecasts actually take this business
Short term headlines focus on tools and partnerships. The bigger swing comes from where credible multi year projections suggest Synopsys could end up, and what would need to go right or wrong on the way there. See where analysts expect Synopsys to be in a few years.

Even At Today’s Multiples I Keep Adding Synopsys Over And Over
Before a single AI chip reaches a fab, it passes through Synopsys software, and that chokepoint keeps getting harder to route around. Here is why a stretched valuation, ten billion dollars of acquisition debt, and slowing EDA growth have not…
Published October 7, 2026, 7:15am ET · 2 min read
The intricate architecture of a modern semiconductor chip, representing the advanced complexity in design that companies like Synopsys are mastering to drive technological innovation. © MF3d / Getty Images
I have added Synopsys (NASDAQ:SNPS | SNPS Price Prediction) after every earnings report this year. Before any AI chip reaches a fab, engineers design, verify, and sign off on it using Synopsys software. Each new chip generation is harder to build, requiring more tools, licenses, and simulation. I want to own that toll road for the next decade.
Fiscal Q3 revenue reached $2.48B, up 42.4% YoY. Non-GAAP EPS of $3.91 beat the $3.67 consensus by 6.44%, which makes four straight beats. Management then raised full-year guidance for the second time. Non-GAAP EPS guidance has been raised to $15.04 to $15.10, up from an original $14.38 to $14.46, and free cash flow guidance is about $2.6B.
Ansys is pulling its weight. Management expects it to contribute about $2.98 billion this year, $20 million above prior guidance. The company targets $400 million in cost synergies by year four. Joint products like Multiphysics Fusion should add to EDA growth in fiscal 2027.
EDA runs as a duopoly. Backlog stood at $10.9 billion at Q3 end. CEO Sassine Ghazi noted: “Customers will not invest hundreds of millions of dollars in a product without having the confidence that it is going to work.” Synopsys won more than 95% of PCIe 7 opportunities, and its die-to-die business is on pace to double.
Why My Money Goes Here Instead of Cadence
Cadence Design Systems (NASDAQ:CDNS) is the alternative. Cadence trades at a forward P/E of 32 and 16.68 times sales. Synopsys trades at a forward P/E of 23 and 9.94 times sales. The stock rose 21.7% last week to $505.17, and even at that price it sits near 27x the $18.583 fiscal 2027 consensus.
Debt and Integration Risks I Refuse to Ignore
Ansys left Synopsys carrying about $10 billion of debt. Restructuring charges should total $200M to $250M this fiscal year, and roughly $403M of quarterly amortization drives the trailing P/E to 86. China export controls, a short customer list, and shareholder lawsuits over Design IP add risk. Q3 EDA growth slowed to 8.5%.
None of that has changed my thesis. Management repaid $3.46B of debt in the first half and paid off term loans early. Total liabilities fell 19.6% YoY, and cash rose to $3.61B. Double-digit organic EDA growth is also expected in Q4 and for the full year.
Analysts made 18 upward revisions to fiscal 2027 EPS over the past seven days, with none lower. Royalty-based custom IP, agentic AI workflows, and joint Ansys products sit ahead. Synopsys pays no dividend. The stock has returned 752.46% over ten years. Chips keep getting harder to design, Synopsys sends a bill for every added layer of difficulty, and I expect to own a bigger share of those bills.

Synopsys and Amazon Web Services on Wednesday said that Amazon.com's cloud computing unit has entered a multi-year deal worth more than $1 billion to license chip design intellectual property from Synopsys.
Synopsys makes software for designing complex computer chips, helping firms such as Nvidia and Intel decide how to lay out tens of billions of transistors on a few square millimeters of silicon.
But it also increasingly licenses blueprints for parts of a chip, a business that brought in $1.75 billion in revenue in its most recent fiscal year and where it competes against Arm Holdings.
In its early stages, the Synopsys design licensing business focused on common parts of chips where customers found it more cost-effective to license blueprints from Synopsys than to design those parts from scratch. But Synopsys has moved into more complex designs such as computing cores and said the deal on Wednesday will focus on blueprints optimized for specific types of chips.
AWS designs a variety of its own chips, including its Graviton central processors and its Trainium AI chips. The two parties did not specify which AWS chips will use Synopsys blueprints.
As part of the deal, Synopsys will also adopt AWS computing and storage services, as well as Amazon Bedrock to build and deploy AI applications.

Is Synopsys Back from the Dead? EDA Leader Inks Deals With Amazon and OpenAI
Leo Miller - MarketBeat - Sat Oct 10, 7:05AM CDT
Electronic design automation (EDA) company Synopsys (NASDAQ: SNPS) has recently experienced a resurgence in investor sentiment. Through mid-September, Synopsys shares were down more than 20% year-to-date (YTD). Since hitting its September low, the stock has surged more than 30%, putting shares in the green for the year.
Several key developments have aided the stock’s recovery, including an over $1 billion deal with Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) and a development deal with OpenAI. These events signal a potential inflection point in the stock’s trajectory, as Synopsys has so far been a chronic underperformer during the AI investment wave.
Understanding Synopsys’ Underperformance
Synopsys’ poor 2026 performance has been a microcosm of its longer-term underperformance during the AI investment era. From the beginning of 2023 through its September low, Synopsys shares returned just 15%. The stock’s recent surge lifts this figure to approximately 56%, but this is still far from impressive. Over the same period, the S&P 500’s return is approximately 110%, and the S&P 500 tech sector has returned around 225%.
Synopsys’ underperformance has been due to several factors. This includes weakness at Intel’s (NASDAQ: INTC) Foundry business, which has faced delays and has struggled to secure large contracts for its most advanced nodes. This hurts Synopsys’ intellectual property (IP) business because it invested significantly in developing these chips, but it only receives payment once customers commit to Intel’s technology.
There has also been a fear among some investors that AI tools could supplant current EDA tools, hurting demand longer-term. Luckily for Synopsys, the firm’s latest developments push back on these risks.

SUNNYVALE, Calif. – Oct. 5, 2026 – Synopsys, Inc. (Nasdaq: SNPS) today announced that it has entered into an
accelerated share repurchase agreement (ASR) with JPMorgan Chase Bank, National Association to repurchase an aggregate of $1 billion of Synopsys stock.
Under the terms of the ASR, Synopsys will receive an aggregate initial share delivery of approximately 1,735,000 shares, with the remainder, if any, to be
settled on or before January 5, 2027, upon completion of the repurchases. The specific number of shares that Synopsys ultimately repurchases under the ASR will be based on the average of Synopsys’ daily volume-weighted average share
prices during the repurchase period, less a discount.
Synopsys, Inc. (Nasdaq: SNPS) is the leader in engineering solutions from silicon to systems, enabling customers to rapidly innovate AI-powered products. fiscal year 2026. Revenue for the third quarter of fiscal year 2026 was $2.477 billion, compared to $1.740 billion for the third quarter of fiscal year 2025.

Leo Miller - MarketBeat - Sat Oct 10, 7:05AM CDT
Electronic design automation (EDA) company Synopsys (NASDAQ: SNPS) has recently experienced a resurgence in investor sentiment. Synopsys’ poor 2026 performance has been a microcosm of its longer-term underperformance during the AI investment era. From the beginning of 2023 through its September low, Synopsys shares returned just 15%. The stock’s recent surge lifts this figure to approximately 56%, but this is still far from impressive. Over the same period, the S&P 500’s return is approximately 110%, and the S&P 500 tech sector has returned around 225%.
Synopsys’ underperformance has been due to several factors. This includes weakness at Intel’s (NASDAQ: INTC) Foundry business, which has faced delays and has struggled to secure large contracts for its most advanced nodes. This hurts Synopsys’ intellectual property (IP) business because it invested significantly in developing these chips, but it only receives payment once customers commit to Intel’s technology.

Workday has signed a definitive agreement to acquire C1.ai, an agentic identity platform that manages access to enterprise applications and systems for employees and AI agents.
The acquisition will expand Workday’s capabilities beyond managing workforce and agent records by adding identity-governance controls that determine what people and autonomous AI systems can access, when they receive access, and when permissions should be removed.
C1.ai connects with enterprise systems ranging from email and customer relationship management platforms to code repositories, financial applications, and cloud infrastructure. Its platform provisions scoped access, enforces organizational policies, incorporates human approvals, and maintains records of actions taken by people and agents.
Workday sees identity governance becoming increasingly important as businesses deploy more autonomous AI agents. The company cited C1.ai research indicating that 95% of large U.S. companies already use autonomous agents, while Deloitte research found that only 21% of organizations report having mature governance capabilities for those systems.
Workday plans to integrate C1.ai with its existing Agent System of Record. The combination would allow companies to move beyond simply registering and tracking AI agents by governing what those agents can access across Workday and other enterprise applications.
The technology could also automate access management throughout an employee’s lifecycle. When a new hire joins, they could receive permissions to applications such as Slack, Jira, and finance systems, while changes in job responsibilities could automatically trigger corresponding access updates. Permissions could then be removed when an employee leaves.
Similar controls would apply to AI agents. Agents acting on behalf of employees could receive more limited permissions than the person they support, while independently operating agents could be assigned broader but closely monitored access. Retired agents could have permissions revoked immediately rather than retaining access after their work ends.
Workday said the acquisition supports its broader strategy of becoming the identity governance layer for the combined human and AI workforce. The company currently serves more than 11,500 organizations worldwide, including more than 65% of the Fortune 500.
The transaction is expected to close in Workday’s fiscal fourth quarter of 2027, which ends January 31, 2027, subject to customary closing conditions.
Support: BofA Securities is serving as financial advisor to Workday, while Orrick is its legal advisor. Qatalyst is serving as financial advisor to C1.ai, and Ashurst Perkins Coie is serving as legal advisor.
KEY QUOTES:
“Today’s companies run on a combined workforce of people and AI agents. With C1.ai, we’ll help secure that workforce by managing and enforcing exactly who – and what – has access to connected apps and systems, giving each person and agent the right access at the right moment to make work easier, safer, and more compliant.”
Gerrit Kazmaier, President, Product And Technology Of Workday
“Enterprises can’t secure the AI era using yesterday’s IT tickets. Workday is the operational heart of the enterprise, and by bringing C1.ai’s identity governance directly into that core, we’ll be able to manage access for every human and agent in real time – making work faster without making it less secure.”

In the wake of its Sana and C1.ai acquisitions, Workday is increasingly leveraging agentic AI to redefine HR and finance business processes. That’s changing the game—and creating opportunities—for the company’s channel partners, channel chief Bronwyn Hastings tells CRN.
Agentic AI is transforming financial and human resource management business processes and redefining how people work.
Workday, as a leading developer of enterprise finance, HR and payroll applications—and with a couple of agentic AI-related strategic acquisitions under its belt—is now a major player in providing the technology that’s driving that AI-fueled transformation.
And that means Workday’s channel partners, which today account for about 80 percent of Workday application implementations, are playing an increasingly important role in the success of those AI initiatives within many businesses and organizations.
[Related: Workday Launches AI Agent Deluge, Acquires Agentic Identity Startup]
“Partners have always been foundational for Workday,” said Bronwyn Hastings, who joined Workday in July as the company’s global channel chief, discussing the company’s agentic AI strategy in an interview with CRN. “What’s exciting is they’re becoming a core contributor to growth rather than an extension of growth.”
Partners are “being encouraged to lean into these new areas of being able to build agentic AI responses across HR and finance. It’s really allowing them to expand their businesses and [take] a more comprehensive approach to the future of work,” said Hastings (pictured), whose official title is senior vice president of global partners.
Hastings is a channel veteran who has held senior channel management posts at Docusign, UiPath, Google, Citrix, SAP and Oracle. In her interview with CRN, she noted that her resume includes experiences with application, software platform and agentic AI companies.
“Bringing all those three things together and then having the opportunity to define the future of work—who wouldn’t want to be a part of that?” she said.
KPMG, the global consulting and professional services company, is a longtime Workday strategic alliance partner that provides systems integration, cloud deployment and digital transformation services around Workday’s applications. (KPMG also just announced that it is adopting Workday internally as its own human resource management system.)
KPMG “really helps bridge the gap between what the platforms do and what our clients need,” and helps them leverage “the power of those insights and intelligence,” Chris Long, U.S. head of consulting and a principal at KPMG, told CRN. Much of that is provided through the KPMG Powered Delivery methodology, part of the company’s Powered Enterprise transformation framework.
“What we’re hearing from our clients, from an AI perspective, is that they’re really looking to move beyond isolated use cases and really lean into how they leverage the power of the data, the information, that is embedded in these Workday platforms” to meet business transformation goals, Long said.
Channel Impact Of AI Announcements At Workday Rising
This week at the Workday Rising conference in Las Vegas, the company launched a wave of new agentic AI products and platforms including autopilot agents that automate a range of functions across the company’s HR, payroll and financial management cloud applications.
Equally important was the news that Workday had struck a deal to buy C1.ai, a startup developer of leading-edge agentic identity technology for people and agents, in a move to boost the identity and access management capabilities of Workday’s applications.
The C1.ai acquisition deal, expected to be completed by Jan. 31, 2027, complements Workday’s $1.1 billion acquisition of Sana, developer of an AI-native enterprise knowledge management, workplace learning and conversational agent platform, in November 2025. At Rising this week Workday announced that Sana is the new agentic home screen and front-end user experience software for Workday applications.
No less important was Workday’s acquisition earlier this year of Pipedream and its integration platform that gives AI agents the ability to initiate workflows, pull data, and execute tasks across Workday and third-party applications.
The vision, Workday executives said at Rising, is that humans and AI agents will not just work side by side but collaborate within environments such as Workday. And partners will play a major role in making that a reality.
Workday’s AI initiatives provide a way for the company’s partner ecosystem to “become a driving contributor” to its AI strategy, not just a go-to-market extension, and bring value to customers, Hastings said. “It’s a very exciting time for partners to be leaning in with us.”
Workday works with a broad range of channel partners, more than 1,675 altogether, including global systems integrators, VARs and solution providers, MSPs, and ISVs, along with the major hyperscalers and leading data platform companies including Databricks and Snowflake. The company categorizes partners as advisory, innovation, services or MSP partners.
In addition to handling more than 80 percent of Workday implementation projects, partners today also source more than 30 percent of net-new annual contract value, Hastings said, up from a low single-figure percentage just a few years ago.
“It always takes the right partners with the right knowledge to really bring AI and agentic to life for customers with real use cases and real value,” Hastings said. The goal today is to ensure that “partners are deeply embedded with customers” to fully realize the benefits of AI.
KPMG is one of those partners. In addition to implementing Workday, KPMG helps businesses and organizations adopt industry best practices and, more recently, layering AI on top of that as clients look to make optimal use of enterprise data and their employees’ experience to improve decision making, Long said.
“And what’s important to our clients is making sure that they’re getting sustainable results and value from their investments,” he said.
Long said one of the biggest challenges around AI today is building client trust in the technology and its outputs. “CFOs and CROs are really looking to embed AI into everyone’s day-to-day work. And in order to connect it into that business process and help employees take action, you’ve got to have trust in the data,” he said.
PwC, the global professional services giant, also partners with Workday to provide business transformation services around the vendor’s HR and finance applications.
“But now with AI, it’s no longer just about transformation. It’s about agentic AI transformation and how you get there,” said Claudio Valera, global Workday practice leader at PwC, in an interview with CRN. “We’re seeing a lot of activity and a lot of interest and movement in the market right now around how to get value from their investment in Workday when it comes to agentic capabilities and just overall transformation capabilities.”
Expanding Initiatives With ‘Innovation’ Partners
Workday has been especially active over the last two years in expanding the number of “innovation” partners it works with, particularly systems integrators and ISV partners who integrate their products with Workday software (known as “build-with partners,” in Workday parlance) and those who develop products on the Workday platform (called “build-on” partners).
“Starting about two years ago, the way we think about developing, growing, curating the ISV ecosystem has taken on a lot more importance and significance for the growth of our business,” Mark Woollen, group vice president of partner innovation who heads up Workday’s ISV program, told CRN.
Build-on partners, now numbering about 170, develop Workday-native applications that extend the functionality of the vendor’s applications. They can orchestrate business processes for specific vertical industries, for example, or provide analytics capabilities that tap into Workday data for decision support tasks. Many ISVs make their products available through the Workday Marketplace and more than 60 have joined the Workday Agent Partner Network.
Woollen said PwC is one such innovation partner, leveraging its expertise in the healthcare space, for example, to develop a Workday-native physician compensation application.
The new agentic AI capabilities announced at Rising this week continue the evolution of Workday’s software into a “trusted agent platform” that ISVs can use to develop agentic applications.
“This is really important for our partners across the board, and in particular the ISV partners,” Woollen said. “It allows them to bring new innovation, new IP [intellectual property] to our shared clients and customers.”
He cited Auditoria, which develops finance automation software, and Censia, a developer of talent intelligence and workforce analytics apps, as examples of companies building agentic products on Workday. Customers, Woollen said, “need those agentic capabilities from the Auditorias and Censias of the world” while also seeking assurance that “they are trusted and that, effectively, as you’ve heard us say, they’re lawful agents.”
Woollen also stressed the importance to innovation partners of this week’s announcement that Workday is applying the Sana enterprise knowledge, learning and AI agent technology it acquired last year to be the new agentic home screen and front-end user experience software for the company’s cloud applications.
By providing a universal Workday user experience across both Workday and ISV applications, the new interface will make it easier for innovation partners to develop applications that tap into Workday workflows, Woollen said.
Channel chief Hastings noted that partners are very-well aware that agentic AI is disrupting “traditional deployment economics” and have responded by “moving away from routine configuration and maintenance” services and are expanding into higher-value “redesigning business” services such as developing agents for vertical industries, custom workflows, and specific personas such as CFOs.

Third-party AI agents built on Claude and Copilot can tap Workday data directly, raising questions about who captures the value of enterprise automation
Workday spent years becoming the place where companies keep their most sensitive people and money data. Now some customers are reaching that data with AI agents Workday didn’t build.
Tools powered by Anthropic’s Claude and Microsoft’s agent platforms can query Workday records directly, skipping Workday’s own AI products entirely.
Workday sells cloud software for human resources and finance. Its pitch for the AI era has centered on its own agents, which it has rebranded under the name Sana.
The problem is that external agents can do much of the same work. Agents running on Anthropic’s Claude, or built with Microsoft’s Copilot Studio and Azure AI Foundry, can read and act on Workday data without customers ever touching Workday’s AI tools.
The industry term for this risk is disintermediation. Put simply, a middle layer moves in between a vendor and its customers, and the vendor becomes plumbing.
So far, Workday’s own numbers don’t look like a company being sidelined. As of Q2 2026, over 5,500 customers were using Workday’s AI agents, a jump of more than 35% quarter-over-quarter.
Its AI SKUs also contribute close to $600 million in annual recurring revenue. That figure reflects growth of over 200% year-over-year.

Workday’s response: become the gatekeeper
Rather than trying to block outside agents, Workday has moved to govern them. Its main tool is the Agent System of Record, or ASOR.
ASOR works as a registry for AI agents, both Workday’s and everyone else’s. External agents get registered, tracked and overseen, with security controls, permission handling and audit trails built in.
Alongside ASOR sits the Agent Gateway, which handles connections from outside agents. Workday supports interoperability standards including Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent-to-Agent (A2A).
Workday also lets customers decide how external agents get in. Access can be configured as delegate or ambient, depending on permissions. Delegate access generally means an agent acts on behalf of a specific person. Ambient access is broader, letting an agent operate in the background within its granted permissions.
Microsoft is part of this arrangement rather than purely a threat. Under a partnership between the two companies, agents built on Microsoft’s platforms can register in ASOR for unified tracking and governance.
CEO Aneel Bhusri has acknowledged the financial potential in monetizing agent access. Workday has built an Agent Management Hub and APIs designed for configuring external agents, signaling it sees outside agents as a revenue line, not just a security headache.
For investors, the story splits into two tracks. The near-term track looks healthy: a customer count past 5,500, quarterly growth above 35% and AI revenue approaching $600 million.
Workday’s counter is a platform play. If you can’t guarantee customers use your agents, make sure every agent runs through your registry, your gateway and your permission system.
What to watch next: how Workday prices external agent access, how many third-party agents get registered in ASOR, and whether growth in Sana adoption holds its pace as Anthropic and Microsoft tools spread.

SAN FRANCISCO & NEW YORK & LONDON--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct 14, 2026--
Metaview, the Agentic Recruiting Platform trusted by more than 7,000 companies, today announced an expanded two-way integration with Workday, the enterprise AI platform for HR, finance and IT. The announcement builds on Metaview's growing traction among enterprise and Fortune 500 companies, enabling organizations to deploy AI agents across recruiting while maintaining their existing systems, security, and controls.
Workday serves more than 11,500 global customers, including over 65% of the Fortune 500. The expanded integration brings Metaview's AI agents directly into Workday Recruiting, extending beyond sourcing to application review, interviewing, and feedback.
Bringing agentic recruiting into enterprise workflows
Building on Metaview's existing Workday Sourcing integration, recruiting teams can now:
Review applications at scale: Metaview's Application Review Agent assesses inbound applicants and syncs advancement and rejection decisions directly into Workday.
Capture interviews and automate feedback: Metaview generates recruiting-specific notes and automatically fills Workday scorecards using existing interview templates. Interviewers can access notes, recordings, and transcripts through Metaview's browser extension without leaving Workday.
Preserve existing workflows: Approvals, candidate dispositions, and audit trails continue to run when Metaview advances or rejects a candidate.
Enterprise-grade AI orchestration with human oversight
As large organizations move from experimenting with AI to deploying agents across critical business functions, security, governance, and control are essential.
Metaview's platform is designed to meet enterprise requirements, enabling organizations to:
Set clear guardrails defining what agents can and cannot do using company knowledge, policies, and rules.
Maintain human oversight over critical recruiting decisions.
Automatically flag inconsistencies or non-compliant behavior.
Access full audit trails of agent reasoning, actions, and outputs.
Protect candidate data with SOC 2 Type II compliance, SSO, and enterprise privacy controls.
"As Metaview increasingly serves enterprise and Fortune 500 companies, we're focused on making AI agents work within the systems and security requirements these organizations already trust," said Siadhal Magos, co-founder and CEO of Metaview. "With Workday serving more than 65% of the Fortune 500, this integration is an important step in bringing agentic recruiting to the world's largest organizations. We're combining powerful AI orchestration with human oversight, so teams can automate more of the recruiting admin without compromising control."
For enterprises managing thousands of applicants and complex hiring processes, AI agents offer an opportunity to reduce operational work without introducing disconnected tools or sacrificing human judgment.
Mimecast, a customer of both Metaview and Workday, is among the organizations looking to bring more AI capabilities into its existing recruiting infrastructure.
“We've been absolutely blown away by the implementation and integration of Metaview with our ATS Workday. The capabilities have far exceeded what we expected,” said Dave Buford, Director of Talent Acquisition at Mimecast. “We originally came to Metaview for its AI Notetaker, but its sourcing and application review agents are already making a significant impact on our team.”
To develop the Workday integration, Metaview partnered with Kognitiv, a global Workday Services Partner whose own team uses Workday Recruiting and Metaview to hire across more than 10 countries.
“Organizations want recruiting technology that works with the processes they have already built, not around them,” said Kriss Bernhard, Vice President, People and Operations at Kognitiv. “By connecting Metaview’s recruiting capabilities with Workday, our customers can reduce manual handoffs, maintain consistent candidate data and create a seamless experience for both recruiting teams and potential hires.”
To learn more about how to use Metaview and Workday, visit https://www.metaview.ai/resources/blog/metaview-now-fully-integrates-with-workday.

A trusted global Workday Services Partner, Kognitiv delivers post-production support and implementation services designed to maximize lifetime value for Workday customers.
