About seven months later, four of the arrested occupants — Sheldon Norcross, Tyler Shaw, Sierra Lauts and Steven Allen — filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against the city of American Fork and 13 of its police officers, according to a report by The Salt Lake Tribune. They alleged that their First and Fourth Amendment rights were violated during the encounter, according to local news outlet KSL.
The lawsuit included 19 counts that were supported by incriminating records taken from the officers' equipment –– including bodycam and dashcam footage. The plaintiffs, in the opinion of their legal counsel, were repeatedly targeted by American Fork officers without legal justification.
During one roadside stop before the Airbnb arrests, one officer was caught on camera saying, "I was gonna scare him a little bit and let him go, is all I really was gonna do."
While the lawsuit against American Fork is just beginning, much of the actual dispute that started everything has been settled. Because of the nature of the lawsuit, however, if the city loses or settles, the local taxpayers will be the ones who foot the bill.
The Lego collection that led to an armed raid and arrests
The story began with a prized Star Wars Lego collection that belonged to an elderly Oregon man, Ed Mansell, and his son Bryan. They had consigned the collection — which is allegedly worth $80,000, including an ultra-rare Cloud City set valued as high as $10,000 — at an Oregon store branch of Bricks & Minifigs.
The collection vanished between corporate transfers and ownership changes, leaving the family unpaid, according to Courthouse News.
In a bid to recover their collection, the family reached out to Ben Schneider, a Los Angeles YouTuber known as Reckless Ben, whose channel digs into disputes like this one. He offered to help and, together with some local helpers, traveled to American Fork to film a documentary, file lawsuits and serve court papers to an individual connected to the missing Legos.
Schneider, who has 2.6 million YouTube subscribers, posted a video called "I tracked down the thief who stole $200,000 of LEGO."
But Schneider and his helpers ended up with four days of traffic stops, searches and, finally, the raid that landed them all in police questioning.
While none of the four individuals who filed the civil rights lawsuit were ever charged with any crime, Schneider himself faced criminal charges for stalking and residential picketing, according to a news report by ABC4 Utah.
Read More: Vanguard reveals what's coming for U.S. stocks — and it could be bad news for this group of investors
Why taxpayers cover the bill in cases like this
Federal civil rights lawsuits, like the one in this story, run on a federal law known as Section 1983, which lets people sue government officials, including police officers, who violate their constitutional rights.
However, there is a Qualified Immunity that shields government officials from being sued individually for money damages in civil court — and if a judge grants an officer Qualified Immunity early in a lawsuit, the case against that specific officer is completely dismissed.
This may not be the case for the Utah officers in this story.
American Fork Police Chief Cameron Paul publicly admitted the department made errors regarding the warrant affidavit, saying "we didn't do this perfectly" and "several issues weren't handled well, or were handled outside of policy," ABC4.com reported.
Because the chief admitted to procedural errors and officers were recorded admitting intent to scare citizens, the city faces significant legal exposure.
If the court finds the officers acted with reckless disregard for constitutional rights, Qualified Immunity may be stripped.
However, even if an officer loses Qualified Immunity, goes to trial and loses the civil lawsuit, they still rarely pay a dime. This is due to a process called indemnification.
Ultimately, the money used to pay the victims of police misconduct comes out of the city's budget or insurance policies funded by taxpayers, not the individual officer's bank account.
What the Mansell family has recovered so far
According to a Central Oregon Daily article, on Aug. 19, Bricks & Minifigs announced a "comprehensive and amicable resolution of a private civil dispute" with the Mansell family, compensating them with an undisclosed amount and issuing an "unqualified apology."
It stressed the deal was "a compromise of disputed claims, not an admission of liability or wrongdoing."
Bryan Mansell releases all claims against Bricks & Minifigs, which in turn drops its suit against him — but the lawsuits against Reckless Ben still remain active.
A GoFundMe set up by Schneider for Mansell has raised $531,411 of a $550,000 target at the time of writing.

Investors often weigh stable, brick-and-mortar retailers against high-growth digital platforms. Choosing between Advance Auto Parts (AAP +1.03%) and Airbnb (ABNB +0.84%) depends on whether you prioritize value or growth in your portfolio.
Advance Auto Parts focuses on the essential automotive repair market through a vast physical network. Airbnb operates a capital-light digital platform that revolutionized the hospitality industry. While they belong to the same consumer discretionary sector, their business models offer very different paths for long-term investors.
Advance Auto Parts operates as a major provider in the automotive aftermarket, selling parts and accessories to a diverse customer base. The company splits its business between professional installers and do-it-yourself (DIY) customers, with professional sales accounting for approximately 50% of revenue in 2025. It remains a fixture among retail stocks by operating 4,311 stores and supporting nearly 800 independently owned Carquest locations. In January 2026, the company expanded its private-label offerings by launching Argos, a brand designed to capture value-conscious shoppers.
Financial performance has faced headwinds recently as the company navigates a changing retail landscape. According to its latest annual report filed for FY 2025, revenue reached about $8.6 billion, representing a decrease of approximately 5.4% compared to the prior year. Despite the dip in sales, the company reported net income of roughly $44 million for the period. This resulted in a net margin, which measures the percentage of revenue kept as profit, of approximately 0.5%.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 2.4x. This ratio measures financial leverage by comparing total debt to shareholder equity. Its current ratio, which indicates how easily a company can pay its short-term bills using its assets, stood at approximately 1.7x. Free cash flow for the fiscal year was negative, at minus-$298.0 million. Free cash flow equals cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures and represents the cash a business generates after accounting for investments in its physical assets.
Airbnb manages a global marketplace that connects hosts with travelers seeking unique stays and experiences. The company does not own the properties listed; instead, it provides the digital infrastructure for more than 5 million hosts to list their homes. This capital-light model allows the platform to scale rapidly across 220 countries and regions. By focusing on a two-sided network, the company benefits from a self-sustaining cycle where more hosts attract more guests, and vice versa.
Growth remains a central theme for the travel leader as it expands its international footprint. In FY 2025, revenue reached about $12.3 billion, which indicates a growth rate of approximately 10.3% over the previous year. The company reported net income of roughly $2.5 billion for the same period. This led to a net margin of approximately 20.4%, showing that the company retains a significant portion of its sales as profit after all expenses are paid.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately 0.3x. This indicates a conservative level of debt relative to equity. Its current ratio was roughly 1.4x, suggesting the company maintains sufficient liquidity to meet its near-term obligations. Free cash flow reached nearly $4.6 billion in FY 2025. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 34% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
Advance Auto Parts faces significant competitive threats from national automotive retailers like AutoZone Inc. (AZO +2.01%) and O'Reilly Automotive Inc. (ORLY +1.07%), as well as mass merchandisers like Amazon.com Inc. (AMZN +0.07%). The company is currently exposed to operational risks from its ongoing restructuring efforts, including potential costs from lease terminations and store closures. Furthermore, cybersecurity remains a concern following a previous data breach settlement, while global logistics disruptions and trade tariffs could impact its supply chain stability.
Airbnb is subject to high competitive pressure in the travel industry from search engines and hotel chains, as well as online travel agencies like Booking Holdings Inc. (BKNG +0.81%). The platform faces ongoing regulatory risks as various local and international governments implement short-term rental bans or restrictions. Additionally, the company is exposed to financial risks from its dependence on cloud hosting infrastructure and ongoing legal disputes with tax authorities regarding the valuation of its intellectual property.
Airbnb carries a much higher valuation reflecting its double-digit growth, while Advance Auto Parts trades at a deep discount amid its business turnaround.
Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Advance Auto Parts is in the midst of turning around the struggles it has experienced over the past few years around sales growth, margins, and market share. The aftermarket auto parts business has been in a slump, due largely to a mix of factors: weak do-it-yourselfer demand, vehicle electrification, intense competition, and general pocketbook pressures on consumers.
Company management has been addressing the business' issues by rolling out a new multi-year turnaround program. That started in late 2024, including closing stores, optimizing store footprints, and overhauling its supply chain. To date, the program has produced mixed results. First-quarter fiscal 2026 results that were much better than expected, with revenue of $2.6 billion and net income of $25 million. But the second quarter disappointed the street, and shares plunged as revenue fell short of consensus at $2 billion, even as net income and other metrics beat expectations.
Analysts see full-year 2026 sales a little lower at $8.57 billion, with net income improving to $167 million, roughly four times 2025.
Airbnb reported an excellent second quarter of fiscal 2026, rallying shares sharply after results. The business beat consensus revenue estimates by $100 million, reporting $3.6 billion in sales, up 17% from the same period in 2025, driven by a strong increase in booked nights. Foreign markets like India and Latin America, two markets in which Airbnb is seeking growth, were exceptionally strong. The third quarter should see sales close to $4.8 billion and net income around $1.7 billion.
The business is finding ways to expand its popular travel business, embracing features like buy now, pay later (BNPL) on reservations, a form of short-term lending. The network advantage of Airbnb's history, over 2 billion guest arrivals since 2008, and the lack of host presence on AI (meaning a competitor using AI has little data and information to scrape in order to form a competing product) give it a competitive moat.
For the full year, management expects sales of $14.1 billion with net income of $3.2 billion.
So which stock to choose? In the highly competitive retail sector, Advance Auto Parts is by no means guaranteed success despite its strong efforts to recover. Airbnb's capital-light model also means it has far fewer competitive moats. But it's the healthier and faster-growing business of the two, and until the company can't execute and competitors catch up, it appears to be a long-term buy.

As global travel demand shifts and specialty retail adapts to new consumer habits, investors face a choice between two industry leaders. Should you buy Airbnb (ABNB +0.84%) or DICK'S Sporting Goods (DKS -0.48%)?
Airbnb transformed the travel landscape by connecting hosts and guests globally through its marketplace. DICK'S Sporting Goods has expanded its footprint through strategic acquisitions and a robust physical store network. Both companies cater to discretionary spending but offer vastly different business models, making this a classic match-up between technology and retail.
Airbnb operates as a global marketplace that connects travelers with hosts offering unique stays and experiences in over 220 countries and regions. By facilitating over 9 million active listings without owning the underlying real estate, the company maintains an asset-light model. This approach has allowed it to become a significant presence among travel and tourism stocks.
In its 2025 fiscal year (FY), revenue reached $12.3 billion, representing a growth rate of 10.8% compared to the previous year. This performance resulted in net income of $2.5 billion. The net margin of 20.4% remains high, although it is lower than the figures reported in the previous two fiscal years.
As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company maintained a current ratio of 1.4x, indicating its ability to cover short-term liabilities with short-term assets. The debt-to-equity ratio was 0.3x, showing that total debt was low relative to shareholder equity. Free cash flow for FY 2025 reached $4.6 billion, though stock-based compensation (SBC) represented 34.3% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.
DICK'S Sporting Goods serves a global sports community through banners like Golf Galaxy and its primary retail locations. A major part of its strategy involves a partnership with Nike (NKE +1.80%), which accounts for 31% of its consolidated merchandise purchases. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk, though the company also works with partners like DoorDash (DASH -0.96%) and FedEx (FDX +1.70%) for fulfillment.
In FY 2025, revenue reached $17.2 billion, marking a significant growth rate of 28.1%. Despite this robust sales expansion, the company reported net income of $849.2 million. The net margin for the period was 4.9%, which is a decrease from the levels achieved in the prior two fiscal years.
As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the company reported a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.4x. This metric indicates that the company has $1.40 in total debt for every dollar of shareholder equity. The current ratio stood at 1.5x, while free cash flow for FY 2025 was $400.2 million.
Airbnb faces intense competition from established online travel agencies such as Booking Holdings (BKNG +0.81%) and Expedia Group (EXPE +3.10%). The company also deals with significant regulatory risks regarding short-term rental compliance and ongoing international tax disputes. Management must also navigate potential risks from AI development and operational hurdles related to global expansion.
DICK'S Sporting Goods operates in a fragmented retail market where it competes with other specialty shops. The company manages risks related to inventory shrink and its reliance on Nike, which provides a significant portion of its inventory. Furthermore, any failure to realize anticipated synergies from the Foot Locker acquisition or a decline in consumer spending could impact its long-term financial health.
DICK'S Sporting Goods appears significantly cheaper based on its Forward P/E, while Airbnb carries a premium price for its higher net margin and asset-light model. The P/S ratio measures market capitalization divided by sales over the past twelve months, while the Forward P/E compares the stock price to future earnings estimates.
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Both Airbnb and DICK'S Sporting Goods possess compelling qualities that make them attractive stock investments. I like Airbnb's asset-light model. This allows the company to produce a high net income margin, which was 23% in the second quarter of 2026. That's why I bought shares in the lodging giant. However, its stock price has risen thanks to the travel industry's strong performance this year, making its valuation high.
DICK'S Sporting Goods was doing great until it released results for its fiscal Q2, ended Aug. 1. The company revealed its Foot Locker acquisition underperformed expectations, forcing management to reduce its 2026 full-year outlook. This caused the stock to crash. Shares fell 30% on Aug. 25, the day that earnings were released.
Interestingly, insiders quickly bought shares, suggesting the stock was undervalued at that point. Looking at its sales and forward earnings multiples, which are both near low points for the past year, indicate that shares appear cheap. This is why I would buy DICK'S stock over Airbnb. It has the potential to deliver a larger return than Airbnb right now.

Airbnb (ABNB) Expands AI Travel Tools, Is The Stock Still Undervalued?
Sun, October 18, 2026 at 7:15 AM CDT 5 min read
Airbnb (ABNB) put its fall product update front and center this week, spotlighting AI-powered search and new on-trip services that tighten the link between its travel platform and day-to-day trip logistics.
Recent price action has been broadly supportive of that story, with a 30.59% year to date share price return and a 37.96% total shareholder return over the past year, suggesting that momentum has been building as Airbnb rolls out product upgrades and investors reassess its risk and growth profile.
See how Airbnb's AI-driven travel push fits alongside other fast-moving consumer services by reviewing our hand-picked list of 20 high quality undiscovered gems with strong fundamentals and room for a rerating.
Airbnb now trades close to analyst targets, yet internal fair value estimates still suggest a sizable gap. Is this latest AI-fueled rally already pricing in the story, or is that 40% implied discount too wide?
Most Popular Narrative: 4.5% Undervalued
Airbnb's most followed valuation storyline pegs fair value at $181.84 per share compared with the recent $173.70 close. This points to a modest upside gap that still needs to be justified by the underlying business mix and product momentum.
"This is the first time in a while where Airbnb is not asking investors to believe that the next growth engine is coming. Some of it is actually showing up. Core markets are accelerating again. International markets are still growing quickly. AI is reducing costs. The core product is converting better. Hotels are gaining traction. Experiences are at least moving in the right direction. And profitability remains very strong."
See why 86 investors see Airbnb as 4% undervalued.
According to TickerTickle, that fair value view rests on a few key levers. The narrative uses a 12% annual revenue growth rate, a 24.5% long term net margin and a future P/E of 27x, all discounted at 8.5%. Those inputs combine into a fair value estimate of $181.84, only slightly above the current share price yet still meaningfully below the $290.97 future cash flow value implied by the SWS DCF model.
This creates an interesting split for readers. The DCF output and Simply Wall St valuation checks flag Airbnb as trading 40.3% below future cash flow value. The popular narrative frames the gap as a 4.5% discount to fair value. That tension often reflects different expectations for how quickly earnings and free cash flow convert into shareholder returns, rather than a disagreement about the direction of the business itself.
For now, the story that markets seem to be responding to is clear. Airbnb has become profitable, is generating high quality earnings, carries a high 34.5% forecast return on equity in three years and has been using strong free cash flow to fund buybacks and reduce share count. At the same time, earnings are projected to grow 15.55% per year, which is slightly slower than the broader US market, so investors still need to decide how much to pay for that mix of quality and growth.
Result: Fair Value of $181.84 (UNDERVALUED)
Still, tighter regulations in key regions and the unresolved US$1.3b IRS dispute could quickly change how investors view Airbnb's earnings power and valuation story.
Find out about the key risks to this Airbnb narrative.
Another View: Airbnb Looks Expensive On Earnings
Airbnb might look cheap on future cash flows, but its P/E of 38.1x tells a different story. That multiple is above the US Hospitality group at 19.6x and ahead of the 30.5x peer average. It also sits above a 30x fair ratio, which raises clear valuation risk for anyone buying on earnings multiples alone.

How Investors May Respond To Airbnb Stock AI Search Update
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 10:19 PM CDT 4 min read
Airbnb recently rolled out a fall product update that connects travelers with friends' trips, introduces AI-powered search, and adds on-trip services like Instacart grocery delivery, laundry, baby gear rentals, and local experiences.
The tighter integration of AI search with services such as grocery and gear delivery points to Airbnb pushing deeper into higher-fee, non-lodging spend across each trip.
We will now look at how Airbnb's investment narrative is shaped by these AI-powered search upgrades and expanded on-trip services.
Scan beyond Airbnb's AI-fueled travel update and see how other platforms are using data and automation to reshape bookings, logistics, and spend patterns with a curated list of 55 AI infrastructure stocks.
To own Airbnb, you have to believe it can keep turning a global host network, strong direct traffic, and an expanding services layer into consistent earnings while staying ahead of new AI booking agents and regulation. The fall product update sits right on that thesis. It tightens the link between discovery, booking, and on-trip spend, but does not change the core near term driver, which is execution on the broader travel platform vision.
The biggest short term swing factor is how effectively Airbnb can grow higher fee experiences, hotels, and services without eroding guest or host satisfaction. The main risk remains external pressure, from AI intermediaries that could sit between Airbnb and users, and from city level rules that may limit supply. The new features are helpful but not decisive against either issue yet.
The most relevant piece of the recent rollout is the AI powered search that lets you describe a trip in natural language and see homes, experiences, and services in one view. For investors, this speaks directly to two things that matter for Airbnb: how efficiently the marketplace matches supply and demand, and how much of a trip's wallet the platform can realistically capture.
Execution is what counts. If AI summaries and side by side comparisons reduce search friction, guests may be more willing to book longer stays, try hotels on Airbnb, or attach services like grocery delivery and laundry. That supports the existing catalyst around experiences and services raising revenue per booking, but it also raises the bar on product quality. Any mismatch between AI recommendations, actual listings, and on trip services would quickly show up in reviews and support costs.
Airbnb's narrative projects US$18.6b revenue and US$4.7b earnings by 2029. That path assumes revenue growing at 12.3% per year and an earnings increase of about US$2b from US$2.7b today.

One bullish twist on Airbnb focuses on AI driven efficiency. The most optimistic analysts were already penciling in revenue of about US$20.4b and earnings of US$5.3b by 2029, before this fall update. You can treat these as an upper bound and ask whether the new AI search and on trip services could eventually push those views even higher or prompt a rethink. Airbnb's AI update tests the "full travel platform" story

By pulling social trip planning, history from friends and on-trip logistics into its own app, Airbnb is effectively trying to reduce the risk analysts flagged around third party AI agents diluting direct traffic.

Airbnb's Brian Chesky barely writes one email a week — while Uber's CEO expects weekend replies
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 4:00 PM CDT 5 min read
Brian Chesky, 45, the CEO of San Francisco-based home-sharing company Airbnb, [NASDAQ:ABNB] has pretty much given up on writing emails. He still answers the ones that land in his inbox, but when he needs something from his team, he picks up his phone and texts them instead.
"I don't know if I write an email a week," Chesky said in an interview with Time. Texts are a different story, he explained, because, "When you get a text message, it doesn't feel like work to respond."

Among big-company CEOs who've talked publicly about how they communicate, he's in the minority. Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Uber's Dara Khosrowshahi, for example, still do a lot of their managing over email.
Most office workers couldn't skip email if they tried, since Microsoft 365 users get 117 emails a day on average and give most of them less than a minute, according to a report published June by Microsoft.
Chesky told Time that if he had to rank how he likes to communicate, face-to-face conversations would come first, then Zoom, then texting, with email likely in last place. Emails start with a subject line, he pointed out, whereas a text goes straight to someone.
When something needs fixing, he'd rather sit down with the person, call them or fire off a text than open his inbox.
Read More: Vanguard reveals what's coming for U.S. stocks — and it could be bad news for this group of investors
Which CEOs still run their companies by email?
Then there's Huang, 63, CEO of chipmaker Nvidia [NASDAQ:NVDA], who works almost the opposite way. Nvidia staff have long emailed him short notes known inside the company as "Top-5 Things" — each a rundown of what they're working on and noticing. He goes through those notes daily to catch early hints of where the business is heading, The Wall Street Journal reported in December, 2024.
Over at ride-hailing company Uber [NYSE:UBER], CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, 57, wants his staff to answer emails on weekends. On a Feb. 23 episode of The Diary of a CEO, he said anyone who doesn't answer his Saturday email can expect a pointed follow-up from him on Sunday.
Late-night work is creeping up for everyone else, too. The number of meetings kicking off after 8 p.m. rose 16% in a year, according to Microsoft's report, and a typical employee now trades more than 50 messages outside the 9-to-5.
In Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index survey of 31,000 knowledge workers across 31 markets, 48% of employees and 52% of leaders said their work feels "chaotic and fragmented."
How to reach a boss who barely uses email
You can simply ask your manager (maybe during your next one-on-one) where they prefer to read work messages, whether that's email, Slack, Teams, or even texts.
And for anything important, it helps to cover your bases. Any serious communication should be in writing. That would include things like a raise request, a change in your duties, or a deadline you want on record. But there's no harm in sending a quick text to let your boss know it's there. And if you need an answer within the hour, a call or a text is probably your best bet, since that's how Chesky deals with his own urgent problems.
It also pays to find out what your boss expects after hours, because being reachable all the time can wear you down. In a June 2026 analysis, Eurofound, the Dublin-based EU agency that studies working conditions, found that stress at work climbs with how often people are contacted outside their hours. Among workers across the European Union who get contacted every day after hours, 59% say they feel stress at work always or almost always. That falls to 17% among those who are never contacted. The figures come from the agency's 2024 European Working Conditions Survey.
Interestingly enough, managers are more likely than any other group of workers to get those after-hours messages, according to Eurofound.
Chesky, for his part, says he tries not to text people he believes are spending time with family, emergencies aside. If your boss has never said whether they follow a similar rule, it's a fair question to bring up.

What Changed In Airbnb's Story?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 3:23 PM CDT 3 min read
Airbnb (ABNB) stock trades at 38.6 times earnings, against 22.9 for the S&P 500. Shareholders paying that much need to know what they are buying, but there is a twist: what management talks up on its calls has changed. During the fiscal Q3 2024 call, management said it was focused on making hosting just as popular as traveling on Airbnb, which means getting more people to rent out their homes. On the latest call, management made the case for something else. So what is it?
During the fiscal Q2 2026 call in August, management highlighted hotels, saying hotel nights are growing about three times faster than the homes business. The company also described the next stage for Airbnb as a one-stop shop for travel, and said it had expanded Airbnb Services into grocery delivery, car rental, airport pickup and luggage storage.
Before that, hosts were the supply story. Management introduced co-host networks on the fiscal Q3 2024 call as an easy way for a homeowner to find a local host to run the listing. By the fiscal Q2 2025 call, management said 100,000 listings were managed by co-hosts and that the program could lead to millions more homes on Airbnb. Co-hosts did not come up on the latest call, and hotels took the spotlight. Homes still got attention: management said more than 150,000 homes in World Cup host cities were listed on Airbnb for the first time.
How Big Are Hotels Next To Airbnb's Homes?
Hotels still represent a small part of Airbnb. Management said on the fiscal Q2 2026 call that they account for a single-digit percentage of nights booked. As a result, homes still make up the great bulk of what guests book, even with hotel nights growing about three times as fast.
Management said nights and seats booked grew 10% from a year earlier, accelerating from fiscal Q1 2026. Revenue grew 16.5% in fiscal Q2 2026, faster than the 12.7% growth in fiscal Q2 2025.
Should Airbnb Holders Worry About Its Push Into Hotels?
So far the push reads as more reassuring than concerning, because Airbnb as a whole is growing faster, not slower. Revenue over the twelve months to June 2026 grew 13.6%, against 10.2% for the twelve months before. Management also said roughly 35% of first-time hotel guests return to Airbnb to book a home, meaning hotels appear to be bringing new guests to the homes side.
The concern is not hotels, but the supply of homes. In September, the EU set out plans to give European cities more leeway to curb short-term rentals such as Airbnb. On the August call, before those plans came out, management said policy is a risk, but not an existential one.
When Airbnb reports on or around November 5, 2026, the measure to watch is growth in nights and seats booked. Management expects growth at a low double-digit rate for fiscal Q3 2026.
How To Act On ABNB?
Not necessarily on Airbnb alone, if your goal is long-term wealth. Wealth is built by owning the companies that keep outperforming, the leaders of their industries, wherever they are. Here are two companies from Airbnb's own industry that have beaten it. Over the five years to October 2026, Booking Holdings stock rose 69% and Royal Caribbean stock rose 245%, while Airbnb stock rose 2.8%.
Finding companies like these takes comparison across industries and sectors, and that is what the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio does. It holds 30 quality companies in equal weight and, since its inception in September 2020, has returned more than 105%, ahead of a benchmark that combines the S&P 500, S&P Mid-cap and Russell 2000. Lollapalooza festivals, La Liga in Spain, and most recently NASCAR. As we expand these partnerships, we’ll continue strengthening the Airbnb brand and supporting travel demand in destinations around the world. 6
Outlook We’re pleased with the results we’ve delivered in
the first half of 2026, and are excited about the continued traction from our product innovation and strong demand on our platform across all regions that is driving momentum in the second half of 2026. Given this strength, we are raising our
full-year outlook for both revenue growth and Adjusted EBITDA Margin. The uplift in revenue growth and margin reflects the strong demand on our platform, benefits from investments we’ve made in talent, technology, and marketing as well as
strong execution across our product roadmap. We continue to focus on investing behind our growth initiatives. Q3 2026 ¦ We expect to generate revenue of $4.69 billion to $4.77 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 15% to 17%, inclusive
of an approximate three percentage point FX tailwind after factoring in our hedging program. We expect our implied take rate to remain relatively in-line year-over-year. ¦ We expect year-over-year GBV growth to be in the mid teens, driven by
low double-digit growth in Nights and Seats Booked and a moderate increase in ADR due to mix shift and price appreciation. ¦ We expect Adjusted EBITDA to increase year-over-year and Adjusted EBITDA Margin to be down slightly compared to Q3
2025, due to timing of investments. Full-year 2026 ¦ For full-year 2026, we now expect year-over-year revenue growth to improve to at least mid teens, supported by the accelerated pace of Nights and Seats Booked we’ve observed, traction
from product and growth initiatives, as well as continued strong travel demand. ¦ For 2026, we now expect to deliver a full-year Adjusted EBITDA Margin of at least 35.5%— an improvement from 2025 that reflects stronger topline growth and
underlying operating leverage in our core business, while continuing to invest behind opportunities to drive future growth. 7
A CLOSER LOOK Helpful services at your service Great trips include more
than where you stay. Travel is easier when there’s a rental car ready to go, a place to store luggage before check-in, or groceries delivered to your door. These new services are the first of many ways we’re making the whole trip

redesigned the homepage, streamlined the sign-up flow, and introduced more flexible cancellation and expanded payment options. Search and discovery Login and sign-up The personalized homepage helps guests find the perfect home, An entirely new login

HOST SPOTLIGHT More host bookings We added more personalized insights
across the app to help hosts attract bookings, and new tools to better manage and promote their listings. Recommendations and insights Tailored suggestions are built into the app to help hosts improve their listings, attract more bookings, and
increase their earnings. Ee ff ctive pricing Improved earnings dashboard We simplified Airbnb Setup to make it easier for new hosts The new, more insightful dashboard helps hosts track their year- to fine-tune their weekday and weekend pricing.
over-year performance and better understand earnings trends. 10
Business and Financial Performance Q2 2026 148.3M $27.2B Nights and

momentum behind our product roadmap including search and merchandising, pricing and tools, and flexible payments. Additionally, growth continued to be driven in part by our app strategy, with nights booked on our app in Q2 2026 increasing 23%
year-over-year and accounting for 64% of total nights booked—up from 59% in the prior-year period. In addition, we saw year-over-year growth of first-time bookers accelerate to 11% in Q2 2026—the highest in four years—with
continued strong growth in Brazil, Japan, and India. In Q2 2026, GBV was $27.2 billion, representing a year-over-year increase of 16%. On an ex-FX basis, GBV increased 15% year-over-year—two percentage points higher than Q1 2026—driven

The digital finance landscape is shifting as traditional payment giants face off against aggressive new-age banking platforms. Deciding between PayPal (NASDAQ:PYPL) and SoFi Technologies (NASDAQ:SOFI) requires weighing mature cash flow against high-growth disruption.
PayPal remains the dominant force in global checkout, leveraging a massive network of merchants and consumers. SoFi has evolved from a student lender into a full-service digital bank, aiming to capture a larger share of the modern consumer's wallet. Both companies represent different stages of the fintech life cycle, making this a classic value-versus-growth comparison.
PayPal operates a vast two-sided network connecting 439 million active accounts across nearly 200 markets. The company provides branded checkout for consumers via digital wallets like Venmo and unbranded processing for merchants. Merchants also utilize PayPal for unbranded payment processing and "buy now, pay later" solutions to drive sales. By supporting transactions in approximately 140 currencies, it serves as a critical bridge for global commerce.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $33.2 billion, representing year-over-year growth of roughly 4.3%. The company reported net income of $5.2 billion, with a net margin of approximately 15.8%. This growth builds on the momentum from fiscal 2024, when revenue was nearly $31.8 billion and net margin was 13%. This performance shows a steady upward trend in profitability compared to the previous fiscal year.
As of PayPal's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is close to 0.5, indicating that for every dollar of equity, the company has 50 cents of total debt. The current ratio, which measures its ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets, is approximately 1.3. A current ratio above 1 typically suggests that a company has sufficient liquid assets to meet its obligations over the next twelve months. Free cash flow, or cash from operations minus capital expenditures, reached nearly $5.6 billion in fiscal 2025.
SoFi Technologies operates a diversified digital suite offering personal loans, home loans, and brokerage services that distinguish it among fintech stocks. Through its Galileo and Technisys platforms, the company provides banking-as-a-service to other financial institutions. SoFi serves over 15 million members, helping them borrow, save, and invest through a single integrated application. Recently, the bank transitioned its $25 billion annual card program to a stablecoin settlement model using SoFiUSD (SOFID) in partnership with Mastercard (NYSE:MA).
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached roughly $4.8 billion, reflecting approximately 28.8% year-over-year growth. This rapid expansion follows a strong 2024, in which revenue increased from approximately $2.9 billion the previous year to nearly $3.7 billion. The company posted net income of nearly $481.3 million, yielding a net margin of close to 10.1%. While revenue climbed sharply, net income remained relatively stable compared to the $498.7 million reported in the prior year.
As of SoFi's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.2, indicating the company has 20 cents of debt for every dollar of equity. The current ratio is approximately 0.2, meaning short-term liabilities exceed short-term assets. In the banking sector, a lower current ratio is often influenced by how a company manages its deposit liabilities against its loan assets. Free cash flow was negative at nearly $4 billion for the fiscal year, reflecting the heavy capital requirements of its lending and technology expansion.
PayPal faces persistent threats from cyberattacks, data breaches, and system failures, according to its latest annual report filed for the most recent fiscal period. The company is also navigating extensive global regulations and ongoing securities class action lawsuits related to its financial outlook. Furthermore, the termination of acquisition talks with Advent and Stripe in August 2026 has left the company to compete as a stand-alone entity against traditional banks and disruptive rivals.
SoFi Technologies addresses operational risks in its latest annual report, filed for the most recent fiscal period, including difficulties integrating past acquisitions. The business is sensitive to interest rate fluctuations, which can impact loan defaults and the demand for personal lending. Additionally, the company faces regulatory oversight from the Federal Reserve and recent legal challenges involving allegations of trade secret misappropriation from Citizens Bank (NYSE:CFG).
PayPal trades at a lower multiple of future earnings estimates and sales over the past 12 months than SoFi, based on forward P/E and P/S ratios.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?
PayPal's valuation is certainly more attractive here, and conservative investors may appreciate that. However, it appears that shares are cheap for a reason: Revenue growth of just 4% or so is not very impressive.
In contrast, SoFi is growing at a nice clip, with revenue up almost 29% year over year in fiscal 2025. Its net margin doesn't compare favorably to PayPal's, but that is partly due to the fact that the two companies are in different stages of their life cycles. PayPal is relatively mature and established, while SoFi is an upstart in the fintech arena.

Past performance is no indication of future results, of course. Even so, the point of buying individual stocks is the assumption they will outperform the broader market. Neither PayPal nor SoFi has.
If I had to buy one of these fintech specialists, I think SoFi offers better growth potential. But neither company looks especially compelling to me.

What Does PayPal Add to Meta’s Muse?
PayPal has joined Meta’s expanding payments network for Muse, giving users of the personal AI agent another way to complete purchases while extending PayPal’s merchant network into agent-driven shopping.
The integration allows PayPal customers to use Muse to shop and complete purchases at participating PayPal merchants. For Meta, the deal adds another established checkout option as it builds commerce directly into an AI agent that can search for products, interact with websites and act on a user’s instructions.
Muse launched on September 8 and differs from a conventional chatbot because it can perform tasks rather than simply provide answers. The agent can book travel, complete forms and make purchases, including continuing longer tasks in the background while requesting user approval before sensitive actions.
That ability already made payments a central part of Meta’s Muse launch. Adding PayPal now expands the number of merchants and payment credentials that can sit behind those agent-driven transactions.
How Does Muse Complete Purchases?
Meta launched Muse with Stripe’s Link wallet, allowing U.S. consumers to connect saved payment methods and authorize purchases through the agent. Link can complete checkout directly at more than one million businesses that support the service and can generate a single-use virtual card for approved purchases elsewhere.
PayPal gives Muse access to another large payment ecosystem rather than requiring the agent to rely on a single checkout infrastructure. Meta has also integrated Shopify’s Shop Pay and opened Muse to Shopify’s merchant catalog, creating multiple routes through which the agent can move from product discovery to payment.
The model is increasingly important because the competition in AI shopping is moving beyond which assistant can recommend the right product. The harder problem is whether that assistant can actually complete the transaction across enough merchants, payment methods and websites to become useful.
PayPal has already been building toward that model. Its earlier agreement to bring PayPal checkout into ChatGPT connected its merchant network to another AI shopping interface, showing that the company is pursuing distribution across multiple agent platforms rather than betting on one ecosystem.
The strategic value for PayPal is not simply another checkout integration. If consumers increasingly ask AI agents to find products and complete purchases, payment companies will compete to become the infrastructure those agents use automatically. Merchant reach, stored credentials and trusted authorization could become more important than owning the shopping interface itself.
Why Is PayPal Preparing Merchants for AI Agents?
The Muse deal follows PayPal’s September support for WebMCP, an emerging standard designed to make existing merchant websites easier for AI assistants to understand and interact with.
For participating PayPal merchants, WebMCP can expose structured information about products, inventory, carts and checkout to compatible agents without requiring merchants to build a separate AI storefront. The consumer can still approve the payment through PayPal while the agent handles more of the discovery and navigation process.
That matters if agentic commerce develops through the existing web rather than through a handful of closed AI marketplaces. PayPal can potentially make merchants already using its infrastructure accessible to new AI shopping interfaces without forcing those businesses to rebuild their checkout systems.
The payments industry is moving in the same direction. Visa has been developing infrastructure for AI agents to initiate transactions under predefined controls, while a live European test involving Worldline, ING and Visa has already shown that agent-driven purchases can operate within existing banking and authentication rules.
Who Controls the Checkout in Agentic Commerce?
The emerging competition is creating several layers. Meta, OpenAI and other AI companies can control the consumer interface. Shopify and other commerce platforms can provide merchant catalogs. PayPal, Stripe and card networks can provide payment credentials, authorization and settlement.
RelatedPayPal Q2 2026: $1.38 EPS Beat, But Operating Income Fell 8%
No single company necessarily needs to control every layer. For PayPal, that could be an advantage. Its business can benefit whenever an agent sends a customer to a PayPal-supported merchant or uses PayPal to complete the transaction, even if another company owns the AI assistant itself.
The challenge is that the same logic attracts competitors. Stripe’s Link already gives Muse broad checkout coverage, while Shop Pay creates another direct route into Shopify stores. Amazon has taken a different approach by blocking Muse from shopping on its platform, showing that merchant access cannot be assumed.
That makes coverage the immediate battleground. An AI shopping agent becomes more useful as the number of websites, catalogs and payment systems it can transact with increases. By adding PayPal, Meta is expanding that reach, while PayPal is making sure its merchant network remains part of the transaction if shopping begins moving from browser tabs to AI agents.

What Could A PayPal Holdings (PYPL) All Stock Takeover Mean For Investors?
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 10:20 PM CDT 3 min read
PayPal Holdings (NasdaqGS: PYPL) is again the subject of takeover talk, with renewed rumors of an all stock bid by a West Coast tech acquirer.
People familiar with the situation describe the potential buyer as a large listed technology group, though its identity has not been disclosed.
Market commentary on 20 October 2026 points to early stage discussions, with no formal offer reported and terms yet to be negotiated.
The renewed all stock acquisition speculation around PayPal is only one piece of a broader story investors should weigh. Our analysis turns up 3 other big wins for PayPal Holdings as well.
The fresh M&A chatter around PayPal puts a spotlight on digital payments more broadly, which sends many investors toward 10 elite penny stocks with strong financials.

How could an all stock bid change PayPal's position in digital payments?
An all stock offer from a larger West Coast tech buyer would plug PayPal's payments rails into a wider ecosystem of apps, data and user accounts. That could deepen how PayPal is embedded in checkout, subscriptions and AI driven shopping, while also tying its fortunes more closely to the acquirer's strategic priorities and share price.
Does this renewed M&A talk change the PayPal Holdings Narrative?
The current Narrative already leans on cost savings, Venmo, Braintree and new payment flows like AI agent checkout rather than a pure branded checkout recovery. Takeover speculation does not rewrite that, but it does spotlight whether the buyer believes those same catalysts, including the multi year technology modernization program and financial services mix shift, can support the business at larger scale.

What is the clearest near term signal that this M&A story is real and not just noise?
The first hard test will be whether either PayPal or a potential suitor confirms talks or a formal proposal ahead of or around PayPal's 27 October Q3 earnings date. Concrete disclosure on terms, deal structure or a rejected approach would matter far more than rumor driven price moves.
The PayPal story that hides in the boardroom

PayPal just landed a checkout deal with Meta and another surprise partnership that sent shares jumping, but the stock is still down more than 20% over the past year and facing real headwinds that could define whether this rally sticks…

PayPal (NASDAQ:PYPL | PYPL Price Prediction) shareholders have reason to cheer the Meta partnership, but the real question is whether one-tap checkout on Facebook can move a stock grinding sideways through 2026.
Our 24/7 Wall St. price target is $57.11, versus a current price of $53.45, implying roughly 8.5% upside over 12 months. The model rates this a buy with 90% confidence. This is a valuation-plus-catalyst call on a stock trading at single-digit earnings.
PayPal shares are down 20.77% over the past year and 12.94% in the past month, well below the 52-week high of $78.34 but above the 52-week low of $38.12.
The Meta partnership, announced at Shoptalk 2026, enables one-tap checkout inside the Facebook feed and is expected to eventually extend to Instagram. Barron’s reported PayPal is partnering with Muse, sending shares higher.
Those catalysts land on top of a solid Q2 2026 earnings report. PayPal delivered non-GAAP EPS of $1.38 versus $1.28 expected on revenue of $8.68B (+4.75% YoY), with total payment volume of $486.4B and Venmo TPV up 14%. Management raised full-year non-GAAP EPS guidance to approximately $5.38.
The bull case rests on three legs. First, checkout distribution: the Meta integration plus prior deals with Google, OpenAI, and Perplexity position PayPal as a default rail in social and AI-native commerce.
Second, Venmo monetization, where users of both Venmo debit and Pay with Venmo generate more than nine times higher ARPA than peer-to-peer-only users.
Third, capital return: PayPal repurchased $6 billion of stock on a trailing-12-month basis, shrinking the float into a depressed multiple.
The bull-case one-year price is $65.83, a 25% total return. The high-end 2027 EPS estimate of $6.08 supports a run toward $70 if the multiple re-rates modestly.
The bear thesis: branded checkout grew just 2% currency-neutral in Q2, operating margin contracted 248 basis points, and active accounts remain flat at 439M. A $120 to $140 million transformation charge is expected in H2 2026.
Bulls counter that margin compression reflects reinvestment in Venmo, BNPL, and AI, and free cash flow surged 156.5% YoY to $1.775B. Prediction markets assign only a 13.5% probability of acquisition before 2027. Our bear-case one-year price is $50.27.
Visa (NYSE:V) is the valuation-contrast peer, trading at a premium justified by Q3 FY2026 revenue of $11.63B (+14.4% YoY) and EPS of $3.32, roughly triple PayPal’s growth rate. PayPal’s forward P/E of 9 looks genuinely cheap, but the market is pricing PayPal’s slower growth accurately.
Block (NYSE:XYZ) is the closer comp, with a market cap of roughly $42B. It posted Q2 2026 gross profit of $3.17B, up 25% YoY, and guided to full-year adjusted EPS of $4.02. Block is growing faster; PayPal is more profitable and returns more cash.
The 24/7 Wall St. price target of $57.11 reflects a buy rating with 90% confidence. The key factor is the mismatch between a forward P/E of 9 and a company generating $1.8 billion in quarterly free cash flow while shrinking the float.
The bull thesis strengthens if branded checkout growth accelerates into the mid-single digits in Q4 and Venmo monetization continues compounding. The bear thesis reasserts itself if H2 transformation charges expand or Meta and Muse deals fail to translate into measurable TPV lift by early 2027.
These projections assume PayPal continues executing on its transformation plan. Significant upside could come from agentic-commerce revenue materializing faster than expected, while downside risk centers on further branded-checkout erosion or a competitive response from Apple Pay and Stripe.

PayPal (PYPL +1.11%), one of the world's largest digital payment companies, was once a popular growth stock. But if you had invested $1,000 in PayPal when it reached its record high on July 23, 2021, your investment would only be worth $187 today. Let's see why its stock has plummeted over the past five years and whether it's worth a fresh $1,000 investment today.
Image source: PayPal.
What happened to PayPal?
PayPal hosted 439 million active accounts in the second quarter of 2026, but that was just 0.3% growth from a year earlier. Since the end of 2022, it's only gained 4 million new accounts.
PayPal is struggling to gain new users due to intense competition from other digital payment platforms. To offset that pressure, it's relying more heavily on its unbranded payment processing platform, Braintree, and its peer-to-peer payments platform, Venmo.
Market capMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.$48.88B
However, those platforms generate lower take rates (the percentage of each transaction retained as revenue) than its namesake services. As a result, PayPal's transaction take rate has declined every year since its spin-off from eBay (EBAY +0.60%) in 2015. eBay's decision to replace PayPal with Adyen (ADYEY +0.29%) as its preferred payment provider, implemented in stages from 2018 to 2023, made it even harder for PayPal to acquire new accounts.
PayPal's revenue rose 8% in 2023, 7% in 2024, and 4% in 2025. That deceleration indicated its high-growth days were over, so it focused on cutting costs to stabilize its margins and buying back more shares to boost its EPS. Instead of aggressively pursuing new accounts, PayPal rolled out additional features to increase its total transactions and revenue per existing user.
Is PayPal a worthwhile investment today?
At its peak, PayPal's stock traded at 87 times the $3.52 in EPS it would generate in 2021. Today, it trades at just 11 times this year's EPS -- even though its business is gradually stabilizing.
From 2025 to 2028, analysts expect PayPal's revenue and EPS to grow at CAGRs of 5% and 4%, respectively, as it deepens its partnerships with credit card companies, rolls out new services for brick-and-mortar businesses, expands Venmo's reach, and diversifies its platform with more crypto trading tools, high-yield savings accounts, and stablecoin-powered transfers.
PayPal isn't down for the count yet, and its low multiple should limit its downside potential. Therefore, it should be a safe place to park a fresh $1,000 investment -- but I wouldn't touch it unless it raises its paltry forward dividend yield of 1%. As a cheap, high-yielding dividend stock, PayPal might attract more investors willing to overlook its other glaring weaknesses.

Paypal (PYPL) is expected to deliver a year-over-year decline in earnings on higher revenues when it reports results for the quarter ended September 2026. This widely-known consensus outlook gives a good sense of the company's earnings picture, but how the actual results compare to these estimates is a powerful factor that could impact its near-term stock price.
The stock might move higher if these key numbers top expectations in the upcoming earnings report, which is expected to be released on October 27. On the other hand, if they miss, the stock may move lower.
While the sustainability of the immediate price change and future earnings expectations will mostly depend on management's discussion of business conditions on the earnings call, it's worth handicapping the probability of a positive EPS surprise.
This technology platform and digital payments company is expected to post quarterly earnings of $1.31 per share in its upcoming report, which represents a year-over-year change of -2.2%.
Revenues are expected to be $8.7 billion, up 3.4% from the year-ago quarter.
The consensus EPS estimate for the quarter has been revised 0.12% higher over the last 30 days to the current level. This is essentially a reflection of how the covering analysts have collectively reassessed their initial estimates over this period.
Investors should keep in mind that an aggregate change may not always reflect the direction of estimate revisions by each of the covering analysts.
Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise Chart for PYPL
Estimate revisions ahead of a company's earnings release offer clues to the business conditions for the period whose results are coming out. Our proprietary surprise prediction model -- the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction) -- has this insight at its core.
The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a more recent version of the Zacks Consensus EPS estimate. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.
Thus, a positive or negative Earnings ESP reading theoretically indicates the likely deviation of the actual earnings from the consensus estimate. However, the model's predictive power is significant for positive ESP readings only.
A positive Earnings ESP is a strong predictor of an earnings beat, particularly when combined with a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), 2 (Buy) or 3 (Hold). Our research shows that stocks with this combination produce a positive surprise nearly 70% of the time, and a solid Zacks Rank actually increases the predictive power of Earnings ESP.
Please note that a negative Earnings ESP reading is not indicative of an earnings miss. Our research shows that it is difficult to predict an earnings beat with any degree of confidence for stocks with negative Earnings ESP readings and/or Zacks Rank of 4 (Sell) or 5 (Strong Sell).
How Have the Numbers Shaped Up for Paypal?
For Paypal, the Most Accurate Estimate is lower than the Zacks Consensus Estimate, suggesting that analysts have recently become bearish on the company's earnings prospects. This has resulted in an Earnings ESP of -3.18%.
On the other hand, the stock currently carries a Zacks Rank of #4.
So, this combination makes it difficult to conclusively predict that Paypal will beat the consensus EPS estimate.
Does Earnings Surprise History Hold Any Clue?
Analysts often consider to what extent a company has been able to match consensus estimates in the past while calculating their estimates for its future earnings. So, it's worth taking a look at the surprise history for gauging its influence on the upcoming number.
For the last reported quarter, it was expected that Paypal would post earnings of $1.28 per share when it actually produced earnings of $1.38, delivering a surprise of +7.81%.
Over the last four quarters, the company has beaten consensus EPS estimates three times.
An earnings beat or miss may not be the sole basis for a stock moving higher or lower. Many stocks end up losing ground despite an earnings beat due to other factors that disappoint investors. Similarly, unforeseen catalysts help a number of stocks gain despite an earnings miss.
That said, betting on stocks that are expected to beat earnings expectations does increase the odds of success. This is why it's worth checking a company's Earnings ESP and Zacks Rank ahead of its quarterly release. The digital finance landscape is shifting as traditional payment giants face off against aggressive new-age banking platforms. Deciding between PayPal (PYPL +1.11%) and SoFi Technologies (SOFI +2.66%) requires weighing mature cash flow against high-growth disruption.
PayPal remains the dominant force in global checkout, leveraging a massive network of merchants and consumers. SoFi has evolved from a student lender into a full-service digital bank, aiming to capture a larger share of the modern consumer's wallet. Both companies represent different stages of the fintech life cycle, making this a classic value-versus-growth comparison.
PayPal operates a vast two-sided network connecting 439 million active accounts across nearly 200 markets. The company provides branded checkout for consumers via digital wallets like Venmo and unbranded processing for merchants. Merchants also utilize PayPal for unbranded payment processing and "buy now, pay later" solutions to drive sales. By supporting transactions in approximately 140 currencies, it serves as a critical bridge for global commerce.
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $33.2 billion, representing year-over-year growth of roughly 4.3%. The company reported net income of $5.2 billion, with a net margin of approximately 15.8%. This growth builds on the momentum from fiscal 2024, when revenue was nearly $31.8 billion and net margin was 13%. This performance shows a steady upward trend in profitability compared to the previous fiscal year.
As of PayPal's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is close to 0.5, indicating that for every dollar of equity, the company has 50 cents of total debt. The current ratio, which measures its ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets, is approximately 1.3. A current ratio above 1 typically suggests that a company has sufficient liquid assets to meet its obligations over the next twelve months. Free cash flow, or cash from operations minus capital expenditures, reached nearly $5.6 billion in fiscal 2025.
SoFi Technologies operates a diversified digital suite offering personal loans, home loans, and brokerage services that distinguish it among fintech stocks. Through its Galileo and Technisys platforms, the company provides banking-as-a-service to other financial institutions. SoFi serves over 15 million members, helping them borrow, save, and invest through a single integrated application. Recently, the bank transitioned its $25 billion annual card program to a stablecoin settlement model using SoFiUSD (SOFID) in partnership with Mastercard (MA +0.65%).
In fiscal 2025, revenue reached roughly $4.8 billion, reflecting approximately 28.8% year-over-year growth. This rapid expansion follows a strong 2024, in which revenue increased from approximately $2.9 billion the previous year to nearly $3.7 billion. The company posted net income of nearly $481.3 million, yielding a net margin of close to 10.1%. While revenue climbed sharply, net income remained relatively stable compared to the $498.7 million reported in the prior year.
As of SoFi's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.2, indicating the company has 20 cents of debt for every dollar of equity. The current ratio is approximately 0.2, meaning short-term liabilities exceed short-term assets. In the banking sector, a lower current ratio is often influenced by how a company manages its deposit liabilities against its loan assets. Free cash flow was negative at nearly $4 billion for the fiscal year, reflecting the heavy capital requirements of its lending and technology expansion.
PayPal faces persistent threats from cyberattacks, data breaches, and system failures, according to its latest annual report filed for the most recent fiscal period. The company is also navigating extensive global regulations and ongoing securities class action lawsuits related to its financial outlook. Furthermore, the termination of acquisition talks with Advent and Stripe in August 2026 has left the company to compete as a stand-alone entity against traditional banks and disruptive rivals.
SoFi Technologies addresses operational risks in its latest annual report, filed for the most recent fiscal period, including difficulties integrating past acquisitions. The business is sensitive to interest rate fluctuations, which can impact loan defaults and the demand for personal lending. Additionally, the company faces regulatory oversight from the Federal Reserve and recent legal challenges involving allegations of trade secret misappropriation from Citizens Bank (CFG +2.33%).
PayPal trades at a lower multiple of future earnings estimates and sales over the past 12 months than SoFi, based on forward P/E and P/S ratios.

PayPal is relatively mature and established, while SoFi is an upstart in the fintech arena.

Glance previously announced an agentic commerce integration with PayPal that embeds real time product data, cart building and native PayPal checkout for tens of millions of U.S. consumers using Glance powered screens.
The tie up extends merchant storefronts into Glance while keeping PayPal in control of checkout and customer relationships, at a time when slower sales and earnings growth versus peers has increased scrutiny on how effectively the business converts new experiences into transaction margin.
We will look at how PayPal Holdings' investment narrative holds up as the Glance integration tests its ability to reignite growth.

PayPal Holdings Investment Narrative Recap
To own PayPal Holdings, you need to believe the business can turn its large payment network into steadier transaction margins while cost savings actually reach the bottom line. The Glance integration supports this by shortening the path from discovery to checkout on new surfaces. On its own, this announcement does not yet change the near term picture.
The key short term swing factor is still whether PayPal can stabilise branded checkout and keep transaction margin from being diluted by lower take rate products such as Braintree and Venmo. The biggest risk remains execution on the large cost program without slowing product delivery just as new use cases like AI agent checkout are rolling out.
The Glance agentic commerce deal is the announcement most tied to these questions. It plugs PayPal directly into AI driven shopping experiences on mobile and connected TVs, with native checkout and real time product data. That keeps PayPal in control of payment completion while merchants extend their storefronts into Glance through a single connection.
For investors watching catalysts, this integration sits alongside Venmo expansion, Buy Now Pay Later volume and the technology modernisation program. The opportunity is more payment flows running through PayPal rails without heavy new integration work for retailers. The risk is that trust, fraud controls and merchant liability frameworks lag the speed at which these new surfaces go live.
What The Glance Deal Asks You To Believe About PayPal Holdings
PayPal Holdings' narrative projects US$38.7b revenue and US$4.7b earnings by 2029, with analysts building this on 4.3% yearly revenue growth and an earnings decrease of about US$0.2b from US$4.9b today.
The Glance integration sits on top of those consensus assumptions rather than replacing them. Analysts already model revenue climbing at 4.3% a year and earnings moving from US$4.9b today to US$4.7b by 2029, while margin compression plays through. The agent driven commerce story effectively asks you to judge whether routing more AI initiated checkouts through PayPal rails can help defend those profit forecasts in a world where fee pressure and product mix are pulling the opposite way.
On the earnings side, the consensus view is not for a surge. Forecast profit of US$4.7b in 2029 points to a modest step down from earnings today, even as revenues are expected to move toward US$38.7b. That combination of higher top line and lower profit implies analysts see take rates and costs offsetting volume growth, unless new commerce experiences, including Glance, carry enough transaction margin to stabilise the bottom line.
Valuation work ties all of this together. To line up with the current analyst targets, you would be working with 2029 revenue of US$38.7b and earnings of US$4.7b, and a P/E of 10.3x on those forecast profits. That is above the 9.2x multiple implied today for PayPal Holdings but below the 16.4x level cited for the broader US diversified financial peer group.
The gap between the recent share price of US$52.53 and the consensus target of US$56.92 sits at 7.7%. That spread suggests the average analyst view sees the stock as roughly in line with those earnings and revenue paths rather than needing a radical reset. For you as an investor, the Glance rollout becomes one more test of whether PayPal's agent checkout and other new flows can keep the business close to that script instead of forcing another downgrade cycle.

When it comes to fintech enterprises generally, and digital payments companies specifically, PayPal might be the first that enters investors' minds. It has been a leader in this industry for quite some time, particularly in online transactions and money transfers. And it wasn't long ago that it was growing briskly, gains that were accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic.
Between 2015 and 2021, PayPal's revenue was consistently rising at about 15% to 20% per year. It's no surprise that the stock price soared 724% in the five-year period leading up to the all-time high. Then-Chief Executive Officer Dan Schulman even said the business would get to 1 billion users, as he set out to build PayPal into a super app. That playbook was scratched. PayPal went from 377 million users at the end of 2020 to 439 million today, with growth now non-existent.
PayPal's fall from grace has been remarkable. On the one hand, it's still very profitable. And it generates a lot of free cash flow that management plows aggressively into share buybacks.
However, growth has slowed dramatically in one key area, as industry tailwinds faded and intense competition materialized on both the merchant and consumer sides of the business. The company's flagship branded checkout solution has pumped the brakes. Total payment volume (TPV) here increased by 2% during the first and second quarters of 2026 on a year-over-year basis.
During Q2, PayPal's overall TPV grew by 10%. Its transaction margin dollars, a measure of core profitability, increased by just 1%. The company's ability to monetize its established ecosystem is weakening, which is likely what has been harming market sentiment toward the stock.
At a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 9.1, PayPal's valuation has gotten extremely cheap. Investors might be tempted to buy shares. But until profit growth returns and even starts to accelerate, the losing streak could continue.

This trend leads existing customers to sign up for new products and services, thereby increasing stickiness.
The market historically liked SoFi's impressive growth. Investors can now appreciate the company's soaring profits. Adjusted net income jumped 112% year over year in 2025. And it's forecast to rise 72% this year. Improving profitability without sacrificing growth is a powerful force.

PayPal Holdings was slow to make decisions under its prior leadership, with too many management layers bogging down the pace of execution, Chief Executive Enrique Lores said Monday during a discussion at an industry conference.
The digital payments company needs to "simplify how we work, remove (and) accelerate decision makers, reduce management layers, and become a more agile company," Lores said on stage during a conversation about his turnaround plans for PayPal at the annual Money 20/20 financial technology conference.
"We have clarified how decisions need to be made and clarified accountability," said Lores, who was PayPal's chairman before assuming the CEO role on March 1 after Alex Chriss exited. "And having been in business for a long time, I know accountability is one of the most important things to improve performance."
Lores offered a brief summary of some of PayPal's past faults during the discussion, explaining his strategy for the company's turnaround. He spoke with Karen Webster, the chief executive of PYMNTS, a business-to-business publisher.
PayPal's Venmo peer-to-peer fund transfer service and the Braintree processing system "were not getting enough attention, were not getting enough investment, and we have changed that," Lores said.
As part of the turnaround, the company has begun cutting jobs, but has not specified the size of the reductions envisioned under Lores' three-year plan. Bloomberg and the Wall Street Journal reported in May that PayPal aims to reduce its global workforce by about 20% over the restructuring period, citing people familiar with the plans.
San Jose, California-based PayPal also reportedly assessed a potential sale of the business to digital processing peer Stripe and private equity firm Advent International after they made a bid for the company in July. But the suitors abandoned that effort the following month, Bloomberg reported.
Lores did not discuss the sale discussions or the scope of job cuts during his remarks Monday on the second day of the event in Las Vegas
Under Lores, PayPal is betting that a focus on consumer financial services, such as buy now pay later, personal banking and Venmo payments will spark growth and lift its laggard stock price, which has declined about 76% over the past five years.
"The attention of the company has been much more in the merchant side than in the consumer side," he said. "And we are revitalizing what we do for consumers, understanding better what our consumers do, and shaping our portfolio for them."
PayPal also intends to leverage its brand trust with merchants and consumers to capitalize on the expected boom of agentic commerce transactions conducted with consumers' personal agents, he said.
"Trust was very important when e-commerce started," Lores said, referencing the company's roots as an early digital player. "It's going to be even more important in an agentic world, and that's the position that we need to occupy."
PayPal doesn't expect any meaningful sales volumes from agentic commerce until 2028, Lores said, although the company is investing in infrastructure and partnerships to prepare for that growth. "If we are realistic, the amount of commerce that is done through agents in '26, or that will be done in '27, is going to be relatively small," he said.
PayPal has learned that its most engaged and valuable customers "really would like us to offer a broader portfolio of financial services," the CEO said.
PayPal's push into more consumer finance "doesn't mean that we are going to be abandoning checkout," he said. "Checkout will continue to be very relevant, but we have complemented it with an additional portfolio of services."
PayPal is also using the turnaround effort as an opportunity to modernize its internal technology stack, with artificial intelligence helping to accelerate that process, Lores said. "We can do in the next 18 months things that in the past would have taken us three or four years," he said.
